sens: eldest son of Gideon
H3500G.detail: 1. Jether is the eldest son of Gideon, the judge of Israel. In Judges 8:20, after Gideon's victory over the Midianites, he commands his son Jether to kill the captured enemy kings. However, the young man refuses, paralyzed by fear, as he is still a child or too young to carry out this warrior act.
H3500G.origine: The name Jether means "abundance" in Hebrew. It derives from a root that speaks of what exceeds, of what remains in surplus. This name is fitting for a firstborn son, the one who comes first and receives the share of abundance in the family inheritance.
H3500G.emploi: Jether appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 8:20. He is Gideon's firstborn, designated to carry out a prestigious warrior mission: to execute the two Midianite kings captured by his father. This unique appearance reveals a contrast: the son of the great judge who achieved a glorious victory, Jether lacks the necessary courage to continue his father's work. His hesitation creates a moment of tension in the narrative of Gideon's triumph.
H3500G.portee: The figure of Jether reminds us that spiritual courage is not automatically passed down from one generation to the next. Although he is the son of a man whom God chose and strengthened, Jether must confront his own fears. This moment also illustrates the reality of childhood and weakness in the face of responsibilities: God does not ask the impossible. It is a subtle lesson on grace toward those who do not yet have the strength to fulfill what is expected of them.

sens: father of Amasa, commander of Absalom's army
man from the time of the united monarchy in Israel
H3500H.detail: Jether is a character from the Old Testament who appears as the father of Amasa. Amasa became the commander of Absalom's army, the rebellious son of King David (1 Kings 2:5 and 2:32). According to 1 Chronicles 2:17, Jether was an Ishmaelite and married Abigail, who bore Amasa. He is a secondary but important figure as he is part of the history of military leaders in Israel and the conflicts between the various armies during David's reign.
H3500H.origine: The name Jether (יֶתֶר) means "abundance" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of wealth or surplus. It can also be a variant or nickname for Ithra. The name appears in the genealogy of the tribes of Israel, particularly associated with Judah and Asher according to certain passages. It is a name borne by several individuals in the Old Testament, each distinctly identified in the biblical genealogies.
H3500H.emploi: Jether appears three times in the Segond translations, always as the father of Amasa. In 1 Kings 2:5 and 2:32, King Solomon reminds Joab how Joab killed Amasa, son of Jether. These passages place Jether in the context of the civil wars during David's reign, when several men vied for command of the army. In 1 Chronicles 2:17, Jether is explicitly named as an Ishmaelite, highlighting his status as a foreigner integrated into Israel through his marriage to Abigail.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H3500I.detail: Jether is a name borne by several men in the Old Testament, but this one is the son of Jada and brother of Jonathan, descended from Hezron in the tribe of Judah. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2:32 as having died without children.
H3500I.origine: The name Jether means "abundance" in Hebrew, evoking wealth or fullness. This name was borne by several biblical figures at different periods in Israel's history.
H3500I.emploi: This particular Jether appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:32, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as the son of Jada, brother of Jonathan (another Jether from the same passage), and it is noted that he died without descendants. The text of Chronicles focuses on genealogical lineages, and the mention of his death without sons underscores the importance of generations in the continuity of the people of Israel.

sens: Man from the tribe of Judah, son of Ezra
H3500J.detail: 1. Jether is a personal name in the Old Testament. He is a man from the tribe of Judah, son of Ezra, living during the time of the divided monarchy. He is mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 4:17, in a genealogy listing the sons of Ezra: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. His name means "abundance" in Hebrew, suggesting divine blessing or prosperity.
H3500J.origine: The name Jether (יֶתֶר) means "abundance" or "excess" in Hebrew. It comes from a root expressing the idea of what exceeds, of what remains in surplus — an image of wealth and fullness. Several biblical characters have borne this name in the Old Testament, including Moses' father-in-law, Gideon's eldest son, and other figures in Israel's history, but this one specifically concerns a man from the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy.
H3500J.emploi: Jether appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:17, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Judah. He is presented as the son of Ezra and brother of Mered, Epher, and Jalon. This passage is part of the detailed genealogies at the beginning of Chronicles, which trace the history of the families of Judah. No event or particular detail of his life is reported; he is known only by his place in the genealogical tree of his people.

sens: Son of Zophach, from the tribe of Asher, during the divided monarchy
Another name given to Ithran
H3500K.detail:
1. Jether is a man from the tribe of Asher, mentioned in the genealogy of Israel at the time when the kingdom was divided between the North and the South. He is the son of Zophach and the father of three sons: Jephunneh, Pispa, and Ara (1 Chronicles 7:38). His name means "abundance," which evokes blessing and wealth in the Hebrew tradition.

2. In some texts, Jether is also called Ithran, showing that biblical genealogies could designate the same person by slightly different names, a common practice in the Old Testament.
H3500K.origine: The name Jether (יֶתֶר) literally means "abundance" in Hebrew, derived from the root that expresses superabundance or what exceeds. This meaning reflects an expected blessing in Israelite families. The same name has been borne by several important characters in Israel's history: Moses' father-in-law, Gideon's eldest son, and the father of Amasa, commander of Absalom's army.
H3500K.emploi: Jether appears only once in the Segond (1 Chronicles 7:38) in the genealogical list of the tribe of Asher. This mention is part of a long enumeration of the families of this clan, where his three sons are listed. Although little is developed in the biblical text provided, this Jether represents a lineage of warriors from the tribe of Asher, as indicated by the genealogies in Chronicles.

sens: Father-in-law of Moses
H3500L.detail: 1. Jethro is the father-in-law of Moses. He is a man who lived during the time of Egypt and the Exodus, a priest of Midian. Moses fled to Midian after killing an Egyptian, and there he married Zipporah, the daughter of Jethro (Exodus 4:18). Jethro welcomes Moses as a son-in-law and later, when Moses leaves Egypt with the people of Israel, it is Jethro who advises him to organize judges to lighten his burden (Exodus 18).
H3500L.origine: The name Jethro means "abundance" in Hebrew. It is a form of ye.ter. There is also another form of the same name, Jethro (yit.ro), which refers to the same character. In the Bible, this name characterizes a man to whom God granted wealth and wisdom.
H3500L.emploi: Jethro appears in the book of Exodus as the father-in-law who plays an important role in Moses' life. When Moses flees Egypt and takes refuge in Midian, he marries Zipporah, daughter of Jethro. During the confrontation between Moses and Pharaoh, Moses asks Jethro for permission to return to his brothers in Egypt (Exodus 4:18). Later, Jethro meets Moses after the crossing of the Red Sea and helps him organize the people so that they are better governed by judges.
H3500L.portee: Jethro shows how God can use outsiders to guide and counsel His servants. His role as a wise man and priest in Moses' life reminds us that wisdom comes from God alone and must be shared for the good of all. Jethro's example teaches the Christian reader that God often places wise individuals around those He calls, to help them fulfill His will.

sens: Man of the united monarchy period in Israel
Father of Amasa, commander of Absalom's army
H3501.detail:
1. Jithra is a man who lived during the time when David reigned over a unified Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when Absalom revolts against his father King David (2 Samuel 17:25).

2. Jithra is best known as the father of Amasa. Amasa becomes the chief commander of Absalom's army, replacing General Joab. The Bible tells us that Jithra was an Israelite and that he married Abigail, a woman from the royal family (sister of Zeruiah, the mother of Joab). This family connection ties Jithra to the close circle of King David.
H3501.origine: The name Jithra means "abundance" in Hebrew. It is a variant or another name for Jether (H3500), as indicated by the Bible itself. The two forms of the name likely refer to the same person. The root evokes the idea of wealth or profusion.
H3501.emploi: Jithra appears only once in the Scriptures, in 2 Samuel 17:25, during Absalom's rebellion against King David. At this point in the narrative, Absalom replaces Joab with Amasa at the head of his army. It is only through this mention that we learn the identity of Amasa's father. Jithra himself remains an obscure figure, but his name and his marriage to Abigail show that he was connected to the elite of Israel.

sens: What remains, the surplus, the excess
Accumulated wealth, material goods
Prosperity and plenty
H3502.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to what remains after a loss or division — what "is left": in Isaiah 15:7, the inhabitants flee their land and "gather" (that is, hastily collect) what remains of their possessions to take with them.
2. It also means accumulated wealth, the goods one has gathered: in Jeremiah 48:36, the prophet weeps because "all the goods they have gathered are lost" — these riches accumulated over time that Moab sees collapsing.
3. The underlying image is that of abundance and profusion — what exceeds the necessary, the superfluous that accumulates.
H3502.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of exceeding, surpassing. The word appears in contexts where what surpasses, what adds to the ordinary mass becomes visible and striking — hence the idea of visible, tangible wealth, of surplus that can be gathered and transported.
H3502.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Old Testament. In Isaiah 15:7, it describes the remnants of wealth that one flees; in Jeremiah 48:36, the amassed treasures that disappear. In these two passages of prophecies against Moab, the term highlights the painful contrast between past abundance and present ruin: what was meant to remain and accumulate is lost.
H3502.portee: This word reminds us that material wealth — even when laboriously amassed — is fragile and can disappear in an instant. It is a lesson in humility regarding the goods of this world and an invitation not to place our trust in what does not last.

sens: Midianite priest, father-in-law of Moses
Man of faith who recognizes God's action
Wise counselor of the people of Israel
H3503.detail:
1. Jethro is a priest from the land of Midian who becomes the father-in-law of Moses by giving him his daughter Zipporah in marriage. It is with him that Moses tends the flocks before his encounter with God at Mount Horeb (Exodus 3:1). Jethro welcomes Moses into his family and supports him in his mission.
2. He is a man who fears God and recognizes His power. When he hears all that the Lord has done for Moses and for Israel in bringing them out of Egypt, he rejoices and says: "Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods" (Exodus 18:11). His faith is sincere and his words carry weight.
3. Jethro also offers Moses practical advice upon seeing how he judges the people alone: he suggests that he delegate certain matters to capable and God-fearing men, reserving the major cases for himself (Exodus 18:17-23). This advice improves the organization of Israel.
H3503.origine: The name Jethro means "his abundance" or "his excellent thing" in Hebrew. It comes from a root evoking wealth and sufficiency. Jethro is also known as Reuel, which means "friend of God." He is a man from Midian, a region whose inhabitants are reputed to be wise and pious in the biblical narrative.
H3503.emploi: Jethro appears 9 times in the Bible, all in Exodus (chapters 2, 3, 4, and 18). He is first mentioned as the father of Zipporah, whom Moses marries (Exodus 2:18). Then he intervenes as a benevolent father-in-law at the moment when Moses receives his calling: it is with him that Moses tended the flock when God calls him at Horeb (Exodus 3:1, 4:18). Finally, he plays an important role when he joins Moses in the desert with Moses' family (Exodus 18:1-12), where he offers a sacrifice to God and demonstrates his faith. The text constantly describes him as "priest of Midian," emphasizing his religious authority.
H3503.portee: Jethro shows how a man outside the people of God can recognize the divine hand and stand alongside His people. His advice to Moses teaches the importance of delegation and good organization so that the community is well served. Finally, he illustrates how true faith transcends the boundaries of peoples and how God delights in honoring those who recognize Him, even when they are not born into His covenant.

sens: What remains beneficial after the effort, what endures
Concrete benefit, material or moral gain
Superiority, excellence of one thing over another
Persistent utility, what truly serves
H3504.detail:
1. The word describes what remains beneficial and lasting after an effort. It is the "remainder," what subsists as a benefit. In Ecclesiastes 1:3, the Preacher asks: "What advantage does man gain from all his labor?" — he seeks what is truly useful.
2. It is a concrete or moral gain, a utility that justifies the work. In Ecclesiastes 5:8, the advantage for a country is to have "an honored king" — something stable and beneficial.
3. The word also expresses the superiority of one thing over another, excellence. In Ecclesiastes 2:13, "wisdom is better than folly, as light is better than darkness" — wisdom surpasses folly in value and effectiveness.
4. It is the utility that persists and "really pays off." In Ecclesiastes 5:15, the rich man who dies wonders, "What advantage does he have from having worked for the wind?" — nothing remains for him.
H3504.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to remain," "to subsist," "to exceed." The suffix ON forms an abstract noun: literally "what remains." This root evokes the idea of something that persists, that does not evaporate. It is related to the idea of excess: what exceeds, what surpasses, or what remains when everything else disappears.
H3504.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Ecclesiastes (8 times). It is a key word in the Preacher's reflection on the meaning of life. It returns as a haunting question: what is the real purpose of working and toiling if nothing remains? (Ecclesiastes 1:3 and 3:9). In this context, advantage becomes a measure of real and lasting utility — what endures beyond the present moment. Ecclesiastes 2:13 shows that some things have an objective advantage over others: wisdom surpasses folly. But even wisdom or wealth, if pursued solely under the sun, yield no real advantage in death (Ecclesiastes 5:15). The word embodies one of the great questions of the book: what is truly worth it?
H3504.portee: This word invites the reader to seek a meaning in life that transcends the moment and the superficial. It poses the question: do I have lasting results from my work, or am I just vanity? In modern biblical language, it urges us to distinguish the urgent from the truly important, and to seek an advantage that endures — what only a relationship with God can offer. It is an invitation not to waste energy on what fades away.

sens: Fils de Dischon, un chef horite du temps des patriarches
H3506G.detail: Jithran is a character from the Old Testament mentioned twice in the genealogies of the descendants of Esau. He is a Horite (original inhabitant of the region of Edom), the son of Dishon, and he is among the ancestors of the peoples who lived in Canaan before the arrival of Israel. In Genesis 36:26, he is listed as one of the four sons of Dishon, alongside Hemdan, Eshban, and Karen. The same genealogy reappears in 1 Chronicles 1:41, confirming his place in the lineage of Horite clan leaders.
H3506G.origine: The name Jithran literally means "advantage" or "profit" in Hebrew, formed from a root expressing what is advantageous or beneficial. This character belongs to the oldest layer of the populations of Canaan, the Horites, whose genealogies the Bible traces to historically situate the peoples that the Hebrews encountered.
H3506G.emploi: Jithran appears only twice in the Bible, in two parallel genealogies of the Old Testament. The first mention is in Genesis 36, which lists the descendants of Seir the Horite and the kings of Edom, establishing the genealogy of the Canaanite peoples contemporary to the patriarchal era. The second, in 1 Chronicles 1:41, repeats exactly the same genealogy, confirming this historical information. These two appearances do not tell anything particular about his life, but simply place him in the genealogical tree of the Horites.

sens: Prominent part of an animal's liver, notably the caudal portion
Piece of fat offered in sacrifice according to Mosaic law
H3508.detail:
1. The great lobe of the liver is a natural protrusion of this organ, particularly visible in sacrificed animals. It is a part that protrudes, which can be easily grasped and detached from the other viscera, as indicated in Leviticus 3:4: "the great lobe of the liver, which he shall detach near the kidneys." 
2. In the sacrifices of Israelite worship, this lobe was not eaten by the people or the priest, but was entirely offered to God on the altar, burned as a precious fatty portion. Exodus 29:13 mentions it among the fats that are "to be burned on the altar" — a religious act that honors God by giving Him the richest part of the offered animal.
H3508.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to exceed" or "to surpass." The "great lobe" is literally what "protrudes" or "overhangs" — a visible and distinct growth. This anatomical precision shows that the Israelites were well acquainted with the anatomy of the animals they sacrificed and knew how to isolate this part for worship.
H3508.emploi: The term appears eleven times in the Bible, exclusively in the sacrificial codes of Leviticus and Exodus (Exodus 29:13, 29:22; Leviticus 3:4, 3:10, 3:15, 4:9, 7:4, 8:16, 8:25, 9:10, 9:19). It systematically appears in the prescriptions regarding the different types of sacrifices: burnt offerings, peace offerings, and sin offerings. The lobe of the liver is always associated with the kidneys and the surrounding fat — rich visceral parts reserved for God alone. Its constant and technical use shows the importance that the law attributed to this part in the ritual.
H3508.portee: For the Christian, these meticulous prescriptions reveal that God takes seriously what is offered to Him: He does not want just anything, but the firstfruits and the best parts. They also foreshadow the perfect sacrifice of Christ, who gave Himself entirely. These liturgical details remind us that worshiping God cannot be vague or distracted, but requires attentive obedience and a sincere desire to please Him.

sens: Edomite chief from the lineage of Esau
H3509.detail: Jetheth is an Edomite chief or prince, belonging to the lineage of Esau. He is mentioned in the list of Edomite chiefs who governed different territories and clans descended from Esau (Genesis 36:40). His name also appears in 1 Chronicles 1:51, where the same genealogy of Edomite chiefs is listed again. This character represents one of the leading figures of the Edomite people in patriarchal times.
H3509.origine: The name Jetheth (יְתֵת in Hebrew) literally means "a nail" or "a peg." This meaning evokes the idea of something solid and fixed. Like many Edomite names in this genealogy, it comes from the cultural and linguistic context of the ancient Levant peoples.
H3509.emploi: Jetheth is cited only twice in Scripture, both times in parallel genealogical lists: in Genesis 36:40 and in 1 Chronicles 1:51. These two passages enumerate the Edomite chiefs or princes descended from Esau, Jacob's elder brother. Jetheth is listed among other Edomite chiefs like Timna and Alva. These genealogical lists aim to establish the origin and political structure of the Edomite people, who play an important role in the history of ancient Israel as a cousin people and often rivals.

sens: To experience physical pain
To experience moral pain or sadness
To cause suffering or harm
H3510.detail:
1. To experience physical pain: the word describes the concrete sensation of pain affecting the body. In Genesis 34:25, the men of Shechem are "suffering" after their circumcision; they are in bodily pain. Job 5:18 speaks of the wounds that God inflicts and heals: real injuries that cause suffering.
2. To experience moral pain or sadness: beyond the body, the word denotes the inner pain of the soul, the grief that weighs on the heart. In Job 14:22, it is an intimate pain: the man "experiences pain in his body" but also "feels sadness in his soul." Proverbs 14:13 shows that even in the midst of outward joy, the heart can be secretly afflicted and full of sadness.
3. To cause suffering or harm: the verb can also mean to inflict harm, ruin, destroy. In 2 Kings 3:19, fields and springs are "ruined," causing damage. It is the action of making someone suffer or harming either a person or things.
H3510.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the fundamental idea of suffering and pain. The root is found in other words of the Hebrew family that all revolve around the notion of pain, injury, or evil. The word always depicts an affliction — to the body or to the soul — that affects the one who endures it.
H3510.emploi: The verb is used 8 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is primarily found in narrative accounts (Genesis, 2 Kings) to describe concrete bodily suffering, and in the wisdom and poetic books (Job, Psalms, Proverbs) where it denotes rather the inner suffering or pain of the heart. In Genesis 34:25, it is the physical pain of an injury. In Job 14:22, it is the intimate pain of the soul. Proverbs 14:13 shows that the word can qualify the state of the heart hidden beneath an appearance. The sense of "causing harm" also appears (2 Kings 3:19, Ezekiel 13:22 and 28:24).
H3510.portee: This word reminds us that suffering is a reality that God knows and sees. Whether physical or moral, suffering does not escape His attention. Proverbs 14:13 warns us that appearances can be deceiving: behind a smile may hide an afflicted soul. Job 5:18 comforts us by declaring that He who wounds can also heal. This word invites us not to minimize our pain or that of others.

sens: Physical suffering or illness of the body
Grief, sadness, or affliction of the soul
State of continuous, unbearable pain
H3511.detail:
1. Pain can be a suffering of the body: an injury, an illness that hurts. Job is the most striking example — after his misfortunes, he sits on the ground, and his companions see "how great his pain was" (Job 2:13), a pain so visible that it robs him of speech.
2. It is also the suffering of the heart and soul: grief, moral pain, affliction. The psalmist says "my pain was no less intense" even while remaining silent (Psalms 39:3), showing that inner pain can be as intense as anything one might cry out.
3. Finally, it is sometimes an endless suffering, a wound that does not heal. Jeremiah asks, "Why is my pain continuous?" (Jeremiah 15:18), expressing despair in the face of a pain that refuses to cease.
H3511.origine: The Hebrew word keév comes from a root that evokes physical pain. It can denote a wound, a visible bruise. But biblical Hebrew also uses it for any inner, moral, or emotional suffering. It is a simple and powerful word, present mainly in the poetic and prophetic books where the deepest feelings are expressed.
H3511.emploi: This word appears mainly in Job, the Psalms, and the Prophets — where the Bible expresses the cries of the human heart. It describes sometimes physical suffering (Job struck with sores), sometimes moral affliction (the psalmist in silence, God's servants crying in pain). Sometimes it is acute and sudden pain, sometimes a chronic wound that no remedy can heal. Pain is always presented as something real, powerful, that demands a response — whether it be silence, a cry, or lamentation.
H3511.portee: This word reminds us that suffering is a reality that God acknowledges and that the Bible does not hide. It allows us to express before God our truest pains, without pretense. Reading about pain in the Bible reveals that our own sufferings can be brought before the Lord with honesty and that God does not reject those who cry out.

sens: To lose energy, moral strength in the face of a trial or threat
To have a broken heart, crushed by pain or sorrow
To be made sad, weakened by someone or something
H3512A.detail:
1. The word first describes the state of one who loses courage and confidence in the face of an obstacle or danger. It is a form of dejection that takes away the strength to continue. In Daniel 11:30, the conquering king "discouraged" abandons his plan when the ships of Kittim advance against him: he suddenly loses his aggressive momentum.
2. It also refers to a broken heart, crushed under the weight of suffering. Psalm 109:16 speaks of a poor man whose heart is "broken" by persecution and misery — it is an inner rupture, like an object that breaks.
3. The word can finally express the action of making someone sad or afflicted. In Ezekiel 13:22, the false prophets "afflict" the heart of the righteous by deceiving him, meaning they morally wound him and discourage him.
H3512A.origine: The Hebrew root evokes the idea of breaking, shattering, weakening. It is related to words that mean fissure or rupture. The verb can have a passive form (to be broken, to be afflicted) or an active form (to break, to afflict). It is a word that paints the human heart as something fragile, which can break under the blow of illness, injustice, or lies.
H3512A.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always referring to the broken heart or soul. In Psalm 109:16, it is the heart of a persecuted poor man that is broken by misery. In Ezekiel 13:22, it is the prophets who afflict the righteous with their lies. In Daniel 11:30, it is a conquering king who becomes discouraged in the face of a military threat. The word expresses each time a rupture of momentum, a loss of strength — moral, spiritual, or martial.
H3512A.portee: This word reminds us that the human heart, even strong and powerful, can be broken by injustice, illness, or lies. It invites us to recognize the fragility of suffering beings and to treat them with compassion. It also urges us to be careful not to discourage or afflict others through our words or actions — this is a serious moral responsibility.

sens: The hand or paw of an animal armed with claws, a tool for capture
Grip, that which holds someone in its power
H3512B.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the hand or paw of a predator, with its sharp claws — it is the means by which it seizes and masters its prey. In Psalm 10:10, the psalmist describes a wicked man who bends forward to catch the miserable and make them fall into his "claws": the image is that of a feline or bird of prey swooping down on its defenseless victim.
2. By extension, this word evokes any grip, any power that holds someone captive, just as claws hold prey. The claw thus becomes a symbol of domination and cruelty — one is in someone's claws when one is at their mercy.
H3512B.origine: The Hebrew word כָּאֶה comes from a root that expresses the idea of seizing and holding. It belongs to the family of words describing hunting or capturing weapons — in Hebrew, there are several terms for fangs, horns, and claws, each describing the specific threat of a beast. This root evokes the very concrete image of a predator immobilizing its prey.
H3512B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 10:10, where it paints the portrait of a merciless tyrant. The poet shows him bent over, watching the unfortunate, ready to seize him. The context of Psalm 10 is one of lament: the believer cries out to God in the face of the oppression of the wicked, and this detail of the "claws" reinforces the horror of their violence. The word is situated within a theology where only God can rescue His faithful from the claws of their enemies.
H3512B.portee: This word reminds the believer that oppression and domination are characteristic of the wicked. But Psalm 10 does not stop there: it lifts prayer to God, the only one capable of delivering the weak. Meditating on the claws of the tyrant invites the psalmist — and us — not to fear man, but to await justice and protection from the Lord.

sens: To be heavy, to have weight, importance
To be esteemed, to enjoy consideration
To give glory, to celebrate
To treat with respect
To manifest with power and majesty
H3513G.detail:
1. The word first evokes what is heavy, what has weight: a concrete notion that extends to a figurative sense (Exodus 14:4: Pharaoh hardened his heart, which makes it "heavy", insensitive to the voice of God).
2. To be honored is to be esteemed and regarded as valuable by others (Genesis 34:19: Shechem was "considered" by all in his father's house — he had prestige and credit with his family).
3. To honor someone or something is to celebrate it, to give glory through words and actions (Psalms 50:15: "You will glorify me" — thanking God, acknowledging His greatness).
4. It is also to treat with respect, to show submission and deference (Exodus 20:12: "Honor your father and your mother" — to respect and listen to them).
5. When God honors Himself, He manifests in His power and majesty (Isaiah 43:20: the beasts of the field will "glorify" God upon seeing His marvelous works).
H3513G.origine: The Hebrew word kabod comes from a root that means "to be heavy." That is why it designates both what has weight (literal or figurative) and what has value, importance: a renowned person is "heavy" with prestige. The root also produces the noun kabod (glory, honor, wealth), which is omnipresent in the Old Testament. The central idea is that of weight, prestige, what has gravity and dignity.
H3513G.emploi: This verb appears 69 times in the Old Testament. It is used to describe respect for parents (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16), the honor given to God by His creatures (Psalms 50:15; Isaiah 43:20), the glory that a king or leader possesses or earns (Genesis 34:19; 2 Samuel 23:19). It also characterizes the manifestation of divine glory when God reveals Himself (Exodus 14:4, 14:17, 14:18: the glory of God is manifested before Pharaoh). In Proverbs, honoring the poor means recognizing their dignity (Proverbs 14:31). The word changes nuance: it can be passive (to receive honor) or active (to give, to render honor).
H3513G.portee: Honoring reveals to the believer a double responsibility: to respect the image of God in every person, especially the weak and the poor (Proverbs 14:31), and to recognize God Himself as worthy of all glory. It is through honor that we respond to God's call and glorify Him. For the Christian, this word invites us to see beyond appearances, to evaluate beings at their true value, the value that God gives them.

sens: To have significant physical weight, to be massive
To be serious, difficult, unbearable
To render insensitive, numb, harden (the heart or mind)
To enjoy honor and glory, to be esteemed
To burden someone with a heavy responsibility
H3513H.detail:
1. The original meaning is physical: something that weighs heavily, that has weight. But very quickly the word also describes what is serious or difficult to bear — like the burden of iniquities that overwhelms the psalmist (Psalms 38:5: "Like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me").
2. The word also designates the effect of a burden imposed on someone, which crushes them: when King Rehoboam promises to increase the yoke, he makes it "heavy" (1 Kings 12:14), meaning painful and unbearable.
3. A particular usage: to harden. Pharaoh "hardened" his heart (Exodus 9:34), which means to make the heart insensitive, impenetrable, incapable of receiving the word of God — like a heart covered with a thick crust.
4. The word can also express honor and glory: to be heavy with weight is to have prestige, importance, to deserve esteem. It is in this sense that God glorifies His name.
5. Applied to a burden or task, the word means that it is a burden imposed on someone: Nehemiah explains that the reconstruction work in Jerusalem was at the "charge" of the people (Nehemiah 5:18).
H3513H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that primarily evokes physical weight, massiveness. It easily extends to the figurative: what weighs heavily also weighs on the heart, on the mind, on the conscience. The same root produces the noun "glory" (kabôd) — for what is heavy, what matters a lot, what has weight, is also what is glorious, worthy of respect. The Hebrew word thus describes a reality that is both material and spiritual: weight and importance.
H3513H.emploi: The verb appears 32 times in the Old Testament, mostly in historical narratives and the psalms. Its meaning varies according to the context: physical when it concerns a burden or load, moral or spiritual when it relates to the heart. The hardening of Pharaoh's heart is a central theme in Exodus (9:34, 10:1): God "weighs down" his heart so that he refuses to let Israel go, despite the plagues. In the psalms, sin or illness "weighs" on the supplicant (Psalms 38:5). In politics, a king "makes heavy" the yoke or burden imposed on the people (1 Kings 12:14). The word expresses each time the feeling of a force that crushes, makes difficult, or confers weight and importance.
H3513H.portee: This word reveals how the Bible perceives sin and the hardening of the heart: not as a light or inconsequential act, but as something that "weighs," that accumulates, that crushes the conscience and makes man insensitive to God's call. It also shows that true honor does not come from lightness or superficiality, but from what has weight, seriousness, depth — a lesson for the believer on lasting value.

sens: Heavy with weight or content
Difficult to bear or endure
Rich in abundance, numerous or copious
Honored, glorified, clothed with dignity
Insensitive, hardened, closed to understanding
H3513I.detail:
1. In the concrete sense, the word designates what is heavy, what weighs a lot — a physical weight that requires effort. In Proverbs 8:24, the "loaded" springs of water are the swollen, abundant springs, full of their content.

2. It also applies to what is difficult, painful to bear: a burden, a load, a responsibility, or an affliction that weighs on someone.

3. The word also takes on the meaning of rich, abundant, numerous: what is "loaded" with something is filled with it. Nahum 3:15 speaks of locusts "loaded" with numerous specimens, countless.

4. Very often in biblical Hebrew, "to be loaded" or "to weigh" means to be honored and esteemed: one who has weight has importance, dignity. This is the idea that weight and glory go together.

5. Finally, the word can designate what is burdened, thickened, hardened: a heart made heavy becomes insensitive and closed to understanding.
H3513I.origine: The Hebrew root kabod (כָּבֵד) fundamentally evokes weight, physical density. The noun kabod (כָּבוֹד), derived from the same root, means "glory" or "honor": the image is that of weight, substance, of what truly matters. A glorious being has weight, importance, density. This connection between weight and honor is typically Semitic: what is heavy and substantial commands respect.
H3513I.emploi: The verb kabad appears about 114 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with nuances depending on the context. Here, it appears in Proverbs 8:24 (abundant springs) and Nahum 3:15 (numerous locusts), where it means "to be filled with" or "to be copious." In other biblical usages, it describes Pharaoh's heart becoming hard and insensitive, or the honor and glory due to God and the king. The verb changes meaning depending on what is heavy or loaded: a physical weight, a responsibility, an abundance, or dignity.
H3513I.portee: This word reminds us that biblical glory is not light or superficial: it has weight, substance, it truly matters. For the believer, understanding that true honor "weighs" helps to seek the glory that comes from God rather than that of men. It is also an invitation to examine what truly burdens our lives: the real burdens we carry and the true wealth that God entrusts to us.

sens: to become heavy or burdensome
to lose sensitivity, to become dull or insensitive
to make something heavy or difficult to perceive
to harden the heart, to refuse to listen
to be honored, to enjoy glory
to render glorious, to honor
H3513J.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to become heavy or burdensome. It is the weight that adds on, that slows down or immobilizes. In Genesis 48:10, Israel's eyes are "weighed down" by old age — they have become so heavy that he can hardly open them.
2. From this comes the idea of insensitivity: when something is weighed down, it becomes heavy, slow, unresponsive. In Isaiah 59:1, the divine ear is not "too" hard — it is not thickened or closed, but fine and attentive. This means that God always hears.
3. To weigh down can also mean to make difficult to perceive or bear: to make heavy, overwhelming. It is to load something with weight.
4. On a moral and spiritual level, to weigh down one's ears (Zechariah 7:11) means to harden them, to deliberately close them to God's call — as if one were weighing them down so as not to hear.
5. The word also carries a sense of honor and glory: to be weighed down can mean to be loaded with weight, thus to be important, considerable, worthy of respect. One who is heavy with glory is glorious.
6. Hence the active sense: to honor someone, to make them glorious, to load them with weight and dignity.
H3513J.origine: The Hebrew root kabod evokes the fundamental idea of weight and density. A heavy object is kabod. From this naturally flows the sense of importance: what weighs, what matters. Glory, kabod, is the weight, the importance, the density of the divine presence or of a person. The French word "to weigh down" captures well this image of weight that adds on and slows down.
H3513J.emploi: The verb kavad appears three times in the provided passages, but with different usages. In Genesis 48:10, it describes a physical phenomenon: the eyes of an old man become heavy, the vision weakens. In Isaiah 59:1, the word is used to deny: God's ear is not weighed down, it has not become heavy or closed — it remains vigilant. In Zechariah 7:11, the Israelites "hardened" (or weighed down) their ears: they deliberately closed their hearts to the voice of God, making their ears insensitive. Thus, we see the word transition from the physical (heavy eyes) to the spiritual image (hardened heart, refusal to listen).
H3513J.portee: This word teaches us that our capacities to feel, to listen, to see God are not given once and for all. They can become weighed down, worn out, closed — either through age and natural wear, or through our own voluntary hardening. But it also reminds us that God never weighs down: His ear remains always attentive to our cries. It is a call to remain vigilant and to cultivate spiritual listening.

sens: The quality of being heavy, of weighing a lot
Force or intensity that crushes, oppresses
Large quantity, massive abundance
Violence, vehement and destructive character
H3514.detail: 1. The word primarily describes the physical weight of things: in Proverbs 27:3, the stone is heavy and the sand is weighty, but the word also denotes moral or emotional weight — the mood of the fool weighs heavier than all the stones. 2. It then expresses the oppressive force of what burdens: in Isaiah 21:15, a fierce battle is one whose violence crushes those who experience it. 3. It can signify a mass or a large crowd: in Nahum 3:3, there is a multitude of corpses, an impressive accumulation. 4. Finally, it characterizes the violence of an action or emotion: in Isaiah 30:27, the anger of the Lord is a violent fire, a blaze that burns with devastating force.
H3514.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes what is heavy, massive, that has weight. It is linked to the image of a burden, of what weighs on someone or slows their walk. The same family of words in Hebrew also expresses glory and honor — what has weight, value, importance — for what is heavy deserves respect.
H3514.emploi: The word appears four times in the Old Testament, always to express either a concrete weight or an oppressive force. In Proverbs, it measures the weight of things and feelings. In Isaiah, it describes the violence of a battle or the fury of divine anger. In Nahum, it depicts the horror of a massacre with the image of a crowd of dead. Each time, the word creates the impression of an overwhelming power, impossible to ignore.
H3514.portee: This word reminds us that heaviness — physical or moral — has weight in life. Foolish feelings can weigh more than rocks. Divine anger is not a light abstraction: it is real, powerful, terrifying. For the believer, this invites a serious consideration of God's justice and a pursuit of His mercy rather than challenging Him.

sens: Having weight, difficult to lift or carry
Large in quantity, numerous or abundant
Difficult, burdensome, hard to bear
Intense, grave, severe
Lacking liveliness, slow or sluggish
Morally burdensome, oppressive
H3515.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: something heavy, difficult to lift. Exodus 17:12 states that Moses' hands "became heavy" during the battle, as he was tired of holding them up.
2. The word extends to what is abundant or numerous: "There were also with Joseph chariots and horsemen, so that the escort was very numerous" (Genesis 50:9). Here, heavy means imposing by its quantity.
3. It also designates what is difficult or hard to accomplish. Exodus 18:18 tells Moses: "the thing is too heavy for you," as it was too burdensome for him alone — an overwhelming burden.
4. The word can express the gravity or severity of a situation: "the famine was severe in the land" (Genesis 12:10) evokes a heavy calamity.
5. When speaking of the spirit or heart, heavy describes what is weighty, lacking lightness: Exodus 7:14 shows Pharaoh's heart as heavy, closed to persuasion.
6. Sometimes it characterizes what morally burdens or oppresses: "Your father made our yoke heavy... and the heavy yoke that your father laid on us" (2 Chronicles 10:4) — the weight of service becoming unbearable.
H3515.origine: This word comes from a Semitic root that expresses the idea of weight and gravity. The verb from the same family means "to be heavy," and we find related words throughout the Hebrew Bible. The initial image is very concrete: something that weighs, that exerts a downward force. From there, the word has extended to everything that has moral, social, or spiritual weight — what counts, what matters, what burdens.
H3515.emploi: This word appears about forty times in the Old Testament, especially in historical narratives and passages describing difficult situations. It is often found in Exodus, where it qualifies the plagues, the burdens, and the obstacles faced by Israel and Moses. The word applies to both what is physically heavy (heavy hands, numerous escort) and what is morally or spiritually burdensome (heavy yoke, Pharaoh's heavy heart that refuses to listen). In Proverbs 27:3, it describes the weight of injustice. Its nuanced usage shows how biblical Hebrew employed the image of physical weight to speak of what counts, matters, or oppresses.
H3515.portee: This word invites the reader to measure the real weight of things: some burdens are too heavy for us alone (as Moses learns in Exodus 18:18), and we need God's help. It also reminds us that the heart can become heavy, closed, unable to respond to God — a dangerous spiritual condition. For a believer, the word teaches that authentic difficulties are recognized as such in the Bible, and they require assistance.

sens: The internal organ located in the abdomen, the heaviest of the viscera
In sacrifices, the part of the animal offered to God along with the fat and the kidneys
Seat of intense emotions, particularly pain and sorrow
H3516.detail:
1. The liver is the heaviest organ in the animal body, located under the ribs. The Bible often designates it by isolating it from other parts: in sacrifices, the "great lobe of the liver" is burned with the fat surrounding it (Exodus 29:13).

2. During offerings, the liver is ritually separated from the kidneys and presented at the altar as a sacred part (Leviticus 3:4, Leviticus 7:4). This practice shows that certain organs had particular value in Israelite worship.

3. The liver also symbolizes the seat of deep emotions: when Lamentations 2:11 speaks of the liver that "pours out," it refers to the extreme pain of the heart — a sorrow so violent that it seems physically tearing.
H3516.origine: The Hebrew word kabèd comes from a root meaning "heavy" or "weighty." The liver is thus named because it is the most massive organ in the abdomen. This same root is found in the verb "to be heavy" and the adjective "heavy." The liver, by its weight and volume, also metaphorically symbolizes the weight of emotions and suffering.
H3516.emploi: This word appears 14 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the legislative books (Exodus, Leviticus). Most usages concern sacrifices: the liver is always mentioned alongside the kidneys and fat to be burned on the altar (Exodus 29:13, Leviticus 3:4, Leviticus 8:25). A few figurative usages appear in poetry: in Lamentations 2:11 and Ezekiel 21:26, the liver symbolizes the seat of emotion, particularly the pain of mourning or calamity. Proverbs 7:23 uses it to express a sudden death.
H3516.portee: For today's believer, these sacrificial details remind us that the entire offering was sacred for the Israelite — even internal organs had a place in worship. This meticulousness shows the seriousness with which God was honored. The figurative use of the liver, as a seat of pain, also invites us to recognize that deep emotions are real and legitimate in the life of faith: the Bible does not hide sorrow.

sens: That which weighs, that which is heavy and opposes resistance
That which makes movement awkward or laborious
The embarrassment, the obstacle that arises in an action
H3517.detail:
1. The word primarily evokes physical heaviness, that which weighs. In Exodus 14:25, when the Lord "made the march difficult" for the Egyptian chariots, it was because their wheels had become heavy, weighed down by sand or water, as if to paralyze them in their flight.
2. More broadly, this word designates anything that makes an action painful or laborious: that which opposes fluid movement, that which creates an impediment. The chariots could no longer advance easily.
3. In a figurative sense, it is the embarrassment, the obstacle that arises — a difficulty encountered that slows you down or blocks you.
H3517.origine: This word comes from the root "kebéd" (כְּבֵד), which fundamentally means "to be heavy." The suffix "-ut" forms an abstract noun: the quality or state of heaviness. The same root gives "kabéd," the liver (the organ considered heavy), and "kabod," the glory or honorific weight of someone. It is a very concrete image: the heaviness, that which weighs.
H3517.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Exodus 14:25. It is a decisive moment: the Egyptians pursue Israel in the dry sea after the miraculous crossing. Suddenly, their chariots become "difficult" to drive — hindered, weighed down, impeded. This is not a trivial mechanical problem, but a divine intervention that makes deliverance possible. The text explains the mention by the fear that seizes the Egyptians: aware that something abnormal hinders their vehicles, they recognize that the Lord is fighting against them.
H3517.portee: This word reminds us how God sometimes acts in a discreet but effective manner: He does not need spectacular thunder; He makes what should be easy "difficult." For the believer, it is a lesson: when a door seems to close, when a road becomes awkward, it may be the silent action of God protecting or redirecting us. Difficulty then becomes a sign of His presence.

sens: To stop or cease the burning of a fire
To make a light, a flame disappear
Figuratively: to put an end to anger, passion, a threat
To let fade away or die (a life, a lineage, a power)
H3518.detail:
1. The literal sense: to extinguish a fire by removing its fuel or drowning it. It is to stop the combustion. In Leviticus 6:5, the fire on the altar must never be extinguished: the priest must continue to feed it every morning.

2. To extinguish a lamp or light means to plunge it into darkness. In 2 Samuel 21:17, the expression "extinguish the lamp of Israel" means to end the life or reign of King David who illuminates the people.

3. Figuratively, the word applies to the anger of God: to extinguish it means to calm it, to stop it before it ravages. In Jeremiah 4:4, if Judah does not repent, divine anger "burns, without being able to be extinguished." It is an irreversible threat, impossible to stop once it is unleashed.

4. Letting it extinguish: a quarrel calms down in Proverbs 26:20 "for lack of wood, the fire goes out," illustrating how the cessation of conflict naturally extinguishes discord.
H3518.origine: The Hebrew verb קָבָה (kavah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of stopping, suffocating, suppressing. The basic image is that of a fire being suppressed by depriving it of oxygen or by darkening it. The word appears in two forms: one describes the passive state ("to be extinguished"), the other the active action ("to extinguish"). This root is related to words expressing annihilation or deprivation.
H3518.emploi: The verb extinguish appears 24 times in the Old Testament, mainly in legislative texts (Leviticus), historical (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), and prophetic (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel). In the literal sense, it designates the fire of the altar that must never be extinguished (Leviticus 6:5-6), an image of the continuity of worship. In the figurative sense, it mainly applies to divine anger: in Jeremiah 21:12 and Ezekiel 21:3, God ignites a fire of judgment that will not be extinguished, while in Jeremiah 4:4, only repentance can prevent it from burning beyond the point of being extinguished. The word also illustrates the extinction of a life or lineage (the "lamp" of Israel in 2 Samuel 21:17) and the natural end of a quarrel (Proverbs 26:20).
H3518.portee: This word teaches that divine judgment, once triggered by the refusal of repentance, becomes irresistible. It also reminds us that the fire of God's anger burns endlessly for those who reject His grace. Conversely, it affirms that the altar of sacrifice remains lit: God maintains His covenant and His presence. For the believer, it is a call not to let their faith and love "extinguish" (the inverse image), and to fear the anger that can no longer be extinguished once it has begun to burn.

sens: Wealth, material abundance, visible splendor
Honor, dignity, reputation of a person or nation
A shining manifestation of God's power and majesty
Praise, respect, and reverence given to God
Radiant brilliance that inspires admiration
H3519.detail:
1. Wealth and material abundance: the word first designates that which shines, that which is visible and impressive — gold, precious garments, accumulated goods. Jacob acquired great "wealth" (Genesis 31:1), and Solomon asks God for "glory and riches" (1 Chronicles 17:18): it is the abundance that is seen and manifests blessing.
2. Honor and dignity: it is that which elevates a person or a people in the eyes of others. "His head is lifted with glory" (Psalms 112:9) speaks of one whose reputation and prestige grow. Joshua says to Achan: "Give glory to the Lord" (Joshua 7:19), meaning acknowledge His superiority by confessing the truth.
3. The manifestation of divine power: when God shows His glory, it is an explosion of power and majesty that terrifies or amazes. "The glory of the Lord rose from above the cherub" (Ezekiel 11:23): it is the visible splendor of God that fills the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34-35) and the temple (1 Kings 8:11).
4. Praise and reverence: "Declare among the nations His glory" (1 Chronicles 16:24) means to proclaim and celebrate who God is and what He does. Singing His glory is to acknowledge His greatness and give Him the honor due to Him.
5. The radiant brilliance that captivates: glory is that which shines, attracts the gaze, and inspires admiration. It combines beauty, weight, importance — something imposing and magnificent.
H3519.origine: The Hebrew word כָּבוֹד (kavod) comes from a root meaning "to be heavy," "to weigh." The starting image is that of weight, substance: something solid, massive, that truly matters. From this arises the sense of "weight" in a moral sense — importance, authority, prestige. Glory is that which "weighs," that which has weight, that which commands respect. The word has enriched and encompasses both visible wealth, social honor, and especially the majestic manifestation of divine power.
H3519.emploi: The word appears 189 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Pentateuch, historical books, and Psalms. It primarily describes the glory of God: it manifests through spectacular visible phenomena (cloud of fire, dazzling light) during great divine interventions (Exodus 16:10, Numbers 14:10, 1 Kings 8:11). It also speaks of the glory of kings and sages (Solomon receives wealth and glory), and the honor of nations. Its usage progresses: it begins with material abundance ("wealth"), moves through social honor, and culminates in the revelation of divine glory — the idea that God alone deserves eternal and unmatched glory. This is why the Psalms continually invite to "sing His glory": to proclaim among the nations that God is glorious.
H3519.portee: Understanding the "glory of God" transforms faith: it is not an abstraction, but a powerful presence that manifests, impresses, and demands a reaction. For the believer, recognizing the glory of God is to accept that He is incomparably greater, more powerful, more beautiful than anything that exists. It is also to understand that all human glory — wealth, honor, beauty — is borrowed and fragile if not related to God. Finally, the notion of glory invites us to see in the universe and in God's works (Psalms 19:2) a manifestation of His majesty: creation itself tells of His glory.

sens: That shines with brilliance and beauty
That inspires admiration through its richness and magnificence
That testifies to someone's glory and dignity
H3520A.detail: 1. The word primarily designates what visibly shines and catches the eye with its brilliance: the king's daughter is "resplendent" in her gold attire, adorned with her beauty (Psalms 45:14). 2. It applies to what is rich, sumptuous, worthy of admiration: the bed on which the woman sits is "magnificent," an expression of her elevated status (Ezekiel 23:41). 3. It also characterizes what radiates glory and dignity, manifesting splendor and honor: these usages evoke a visible and recognized eminence.
H3520A.origine: The Hebrew word כָּבוֹד (kavod) comes from a root meaning "to be heavy, to weigh"; the primary idea is that of weight and substance, which then shifted to what has weight in the eyes of others, that is, importance, honor, and glory. This same word is very often used in the Bible to denote the glory of God, His majestic and radiant presence.
H3520A.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided Segond translations. In Psalms 45:14, it describes the shining beauty of the king's daughter in her golden adornment. In Ezekiel 23:41, it qualifies the magnificence of a bed, a symbol of wealth and prestige. In both cases, the emphasis is on the dazzling and sumptuous appearance that attracts admiration. This is one of the nuances of the Hebrew word kavod, which in other biblical contexts carries a deeper meaning of divine glory or spiritual honor.
H3520A.portee: This word reminds the reader that earthly beauty, wealth, and brilliance are visible and impressive, but also that true glory — the one celebrated by the Bible — is that of the God who is its source. Observing what shines here below can turn us toward the One who is infinitely more resplendent.

sens: A collection of goods, belongings transported during a journey
Wealth, material resources one possesses and carries along
H3520B.detail:
1. The word designates the collection of belongings and equipment transported while traveling. In Judges 18:21, the fleeing Danites place their luggage in front to protect their family: it is a convoy of material goods, provisions, and precious items that cannot be abandoned.
2. More broadly, it refers to the wealth and possessions accumulated — everything that constitutes a person's or family's wealth. The word emphasizes the weight of material things: it is what costs dearly and is dragged along, what one does not want to part with.
H3520B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be heavy" or "to have weight." This root also expresses the idea of glory and honor, because an important person, rich in goods and resources, "weighs" more in the community. Luggage, therefore, is literally what is heavy to carry — and by extension, what is heavy with value.
H3520B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Judges 18:21. The Danites flee to settle in the north of the land and move with weapons, women, children, and all their belongings. Placing the luggage in front of the group during the march is a tactical measure: to protect the possessions, and thus also the family that depends on them for survival. The context shows people who are relocating, loaded with all they possess.
H3520B.portee: This word reminds a simple yet relevant truth: material wealth is heavy to bear. Even those who possess it must drag it along, defend it, and watch over it. For a believer, it is an invitation not to become too burdened by attachment to goods, but also to recognize that legitimate resources (family, flock, necessary goods) require responsible management and discernment.

sens: City in Galilee, at the border of the territory of Asher
H3521G.detail: 1. Cabul is a city in the region of Galilee, located near the border of the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher during the division of Canaan. It was about 16 km east of Akko (Acre), in the northern part of the Promised Land. Joshua 19:27 mentions it as a landmark in the delineation of the borders of the territory of Asher.
H3521G.origine: The name Cabul literally means "link" or "chain" in Hebrew, an image that may evoke a fortress or a strategic place linking regions together. The ancient site corresponds to the modern locality of Kabul, in northern Galilee.
H3521G.emploi: Cabul appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Joshua. The context is that of the division of Canaan among the twelve tribes of Israel, after the conquest under Joshua. The text meticulously lists the cities and borders of the territory of Asher, and Cabul figures as a reference locality to define the eastern limits of this territory.

sens: District of Galilee given by Solomon to Hiram
Region disdainfully named by the one who received it
H3521H.detail:
1. Cabul is the name of a region in Galilee that King Solomon ceded to King Hiram of Tyre as payment for the assistance provided in the construction of the temple (1 Kings 9:13). It was a territorially significant area in northern Israel.
2. The name reveals a certain disdain: Hiram, upon receiving these cities, would have expressed his disappointment by calling them "land of Cabul" — a derogatory name that, according to the text, "they have retained to this day." The word expresses an implicit criticism: these cities may not have been worth what was expected.
H3521H.origine: The name literally means "link" or "chain" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of "linked" or grouped cities. However, the biblical context suggests that Hiram gave or adopted it as a pejorative term, perhaps with a connotation of aversion or indifference toward this territorial gift.
H3521H.emploi: Cabul appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 9:13. This is the moment when Solomon, after receiving Hiram's help for the construction of the temple and palace, gives him twenty cities in Galilee as payment. Hiram, upon seeing these cities, expresses his dissatisfaction by naming them thus. The account notes that this name has remained attached to the region until the time of the writing of the biblical text.
H3521H.portee: This passage illustrates the tensions and political contracts between the kingdoms of Israel and Tyre, but also the importance of territorial exchanges in consolidating major national projects like the temple. The disdain expressed by Hiram invites the reader to reflect on the value of blessings and the gratitude expected — a subtle lesson on human relationships and alliances.

sens: City of Judah mentioned only once
H3522.detail: Cabbon is a small city in the territory of Judah, in the region of the lowlands (the Shephelah). It appears in the enumeration of cities entrusted to the tribe of Judah during the division of the promised territory (Joshua 15:40), alongside Lachmas and Kithlisch.
H3522.origine: The name Cabbon literally means "the builder" or "one who builds," formed from a Hebrew root that evokes the action of building. It is a typically Hebrew place name, likely designating the founder or character of this locality.
H3522.emploi: Cabbon is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities assigned to Judah (Joshua 15:40). It figures among the many localities in the southern territory, in the hilly region between the mountain of Judah and the coastal plain. Its exact location has not been definitively identified on the archaeological map.

sens: Hide or skin of an animal used as a material object
Garment or covering made from animal skin
Object used to deceive or conceal
H3523.detail:
1. The word refers to the skin or hide of an animal, particularly goat skin — a common material in the ancient East. It is a concrete element of daily life, like the equipment or fabrics of ancient homes. When Michal seeks to deceive the king's messengers (1 Samuel 19:13), she places a goat skin in David's bed: a very real physical object.
2. The skin can serve as a covering, garment, or cloth: it belonged to the material possessions of a household. It could provide protection against the cold or simply be a part of the furnishings. This is the usual domestic use.
3. Through its use in the story of David and Michal, the goat skin becomes an instrument of cunning: placed at the head of the bed, wrapped in a covering, it creates the appearance of a sleeping person, thus deceiving the messengers who were searching for David (1 Samuel 19:16). Here it is merely a disguise, a means of deception.
H3523.origine: The Hebrew word כָּבִיר comes from a root that evokes things that are tied, woven, or interlaced — the idea of a material that intertwines. The word originally designates anything that is assembled, intertwined, or woven together, before taking on the specific meaning of animal skin. This image of interwoven strands fits well with a skin surface, porous and textured.
H3523.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Samuel 19, in the episode where Michal helps David escape from King Saul. She places a goat skin in the bed and wraps it in a covering to make it look like a man sleeping. The king's messengers are deceived by this staging (verses 13 and 16). It is a purely concrete and narrative use: the text mentions the object as part of the scheme. The context of domestic cunning and family protection colors these two unique uses.
H3523.portee: This anecdote shows us how Michal, although the daughter of King Saul, chooses to save her husband David at the risk of her own safety. She uses simple cunning — household objects — to thwart the king's murderous plans. It is a portrait of marital fidelity and quiet courage: she prefers her husband to her family. This humble act, based on everyday material, illustrates how trust and love can inspire acts of great significance.

sens: Who possesses great strength, authority, or power
Who is abundant, considerable in quantity or importance
Who acts with violence or impetuosity
H3524.detail:
1. Powerful designates one who possesses remarkable strength, authority, or superior power. It is the image of the strong, the master, the one who dominates. Job 36:5 says of God: "God is powerful, but he does not reject anyone" — it is divine power, his absolute control over the world.
2. The word also designates that which is abundant, rich, considerable in quantity or importance. Job 15:10 speaks of elders "rich in days," meaning those who have accumulated many years; Job 31:25 mentions "the amount of wealth I had acquired," the material accumulation.
3. Powerful can also qualify that which acts with violent or impetuous force. Job 8:2 asks: "How long will you speak this way, and will the words of your mouth be a mighty wind?" — violent words that strike like a strong wind.
H3524.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of strength and power. In Hebrew, words from this family always evoke solidity, robustness, what is heavy, thick, imposing. The basic image is that of weight, of mass: what weighs heavily is necessarily powerful.
H3524.emploi: This word appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the book of Job. It designates either personal power (that of God, that of the great of the world), or material or temporal abundance, or the intensity of an action or natural force. Job uses it to speak of divine power (36:5), the power of kings (34:17, 34:24), the abundance of riches (31:25), and the violence of the wind (8:2). The prophets use it to describe spectacular natural phenomena (Isaiah 17:12 speaks of a powerful noise).
H3524.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize the absolute power of God, the only truly powerful one, and to understand that all human strength, all wealth, all earthly power is both fragile and subject to his sovereignty. It is a call to humility in the face of true power.

sens: Chain or rope that restrains a prisoner
Shackle that prevents movement
H3525.detail:
1. The word designates a physical bond, a chain or rope used to restrain a captive. In Psalms 105:18, Joseph's "feet are hurt with fetters": it is the concrete instrument of his captivity in Egypt.
2. By extension, it designates any shackle that immobilizes or paralyzes. In Psalms 149:8, it refers to "fetters of iron" to bind kings and nobles: the image evokes a humiliating and total captivity.
H3525.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that designates the action of binding or tightening. It belongs to the family of terms that express constraint and restriction of freedom. The word carries a strongly negative connotation: it never designates a loving or voluntary bond, but always an imposed shackle.
H3525.emploi: This word appears twice in the Psalms, always to describe a real or imagined captivity. In Psalms 105:18, it refers to Joseph's historical imprisonment in Egypt, where he is chained. In Psalms 149:8, it appears in a warrior hymn where the psalmists imagine the enemies of Israel bound with chains of iron. In both cases, the word expresses absolute domination and deprivation of freedom.
H3525.portee: This word reminds us that captivity and oppression are earthly realities that God sees and from which he delivers his faithful. The story of Joseph shows that even in chains, the believer can remain in God's hand, who reverses fate. For the Christian, it also evokes the biblical idea of liberation: we are called to freedom in Christ, not to remain bound.

sens: Worker who washes and treats fabrics
Place where this worker operates
H3526G.detail:
1. The fuller is a worker specialized in washing and treating fabrics, particularly clothing. He cleans the cloth by treading it, that is, by trampling or beating it in water to cleanse and soften it — an intense and necessary manual labor before the fabric can be worn or used.
2. By extension, the word also designates the fuller’s field, that is, the place where this artisan practices his trade. It is a well-known location in or near Jerusalem: the three biblical passages mention the "field of the fuller" as a specific landmark, located near the upper pool, where the Assyrian armies position themselves during their threats against the city (2 Kings 18:17; Isaiah 7:3; Isaiah 36:2).
H3526G.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the action of treading, trampling — that is, treating fabrics through vigorous footwork. This activity was well established in the ancient Near East; it required abundant water, which explains the presence of the fuller’s field near a spring or aqueduct.
H3526G.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always to designate the fuller’s field in Jerusalem. In each occurrence, this place serves as a precise geographical reference during military crises: Isaiah 7:3 and 36:2 locate the Assyrian threat in the same spot, while 2 Kings 18:17 reports the same event in a slightly different form. The context shows that it was an accessible and well-known place, located near water sources outside or on the outskirts of the city.
H3526G.portee: This word reminds us that ancient daily life included specialized trades and well-identified workplaces. It also shows how the Bible anchors great historical and prophetic events in concrete settings familiar to contemporary readers: the fuller’s field is not abstract; it is a place that the inhabitants of Jerusalem could point to.

sens: To wash clothes or the body by rubbing or immersion
To ritually purify someone or something according to the Law
To clean in a figurative sense, to morally or spiritually purify
H3526H.detail:
1. The verb denotes the concrete action of washing clothes by rubbing them, or washing the body. In Genesis 49:11, it evokes the poetic image of washing a garment in wine: it is a rubbing that cleans. The context of Leviticus 14:9 shows a man washing his clothes after his healing — it is a physical act of cleaning.
2. In the Law of Moses, "to wash" becomes an act of ritual purification. One who has touched a corpse, a sick person, or an unclean substance must wash their clothes and body to become pure again (Leviticus 15:11, Numbers 19:10). This external washing signifies the removal of impurity and the return to the state of purity required for the community.
3. The word is also used in a spiritual sense to express forgiveness and the purification of the soul. Psalms 51:4 and 51:9 plead with God: "Wash me... whiter than snow" — it is no longer clothes that are being cleaned, but the heart and conscience of the sinner.
H3526H.origine: The Hebrew word כָּבַס (kavas) primarily denotes the action of washing by treading — the treading of cloth, as done by fullers, is a work that soaks and rubs the fabric. The basic image is that of a repeated movement that cleans deeply. The participle "fuller" or "treader" (one who washes fabrics) is derived directly from it. The word has extended from physical cleaning to ritual cleaning, and then to spiritual purification.
H3526H.emploi: The verb appears 45 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in Leviticus, which codifies the purity laws of Israel. It is used to describe the washing prescribed after contact with impurity: illness, contagion, contact with a corpse, or with unclean materials (Leviticus 13, 14, 15; Numbers 19). Outside of the legal context, it is found in Genesis 49:11 (poetic image of the king washing his garment in wine), in 2 Samuel 19:24 (Mephibosheth who has not washed), and in the Psalms where it becomes a prayer for moral purification (Psalms 51:4 and 51:9, where the psalmist pleads with God to wash him from his sins). Thus, it is a word that moves from the concrete to the ritual, then to the spiritual.
H3526H.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that in the Old Testament, physical cleaning accompanied and signified the return to a state of purity. But the cries of Psalm 51 — "Wash me, wash me" — show that true cleansing is not that of clothes, but that of the conscience. This prepares us to understand that Jesus, in the New Testament, will accomplish true purification through his shed blood, without needing the rituals of Leviticus.

sens: To abound, to multiply in number
To increase in quantity or intensity
To accumulate, to repeat several times
H3527.detail:
1. The word describes the fact that something becomes numerous or abundant: it repeats, it accumulates. In Job 35:16, Job "multiplies" his words — he produces many, without discontinuity or discernment.
2. Used with words or actions, it evokes the idea of accumulation: always adding more, doubling them. Job speaks a lot, unnecessarily; his words multiply without bringing wisdom.
3. The figurative sense extends to anything that increases: actions, words, grievances. To multiply is to grow the number or intensity of something.
H3527.origine: The Hebrew root כָּבַר expresses the idea of abundance and multiplication. It is related to the notion of growth, accumulation. The verb can literally mean "to be many" or "to become numerous." The form used here (Hiphil) carries the causative sense: not only does something become numerous, but someone makes it numerous, intentionally increasing it.
H3527.emploi: The word appears only once in the provided biblical text: in Job 35:16. In this passage, Elihu criticizes Job by saying that he "multiplies his words without understanding." It is an accusation of excessive words devoid of meaning. The context is that of a theological controversy: Job justifies his innocence through many speeches, but in Elihu's eyes, this abundance of speech brings no wisdom. The word thus emphasizes the repetitive and excessive nature of what Job states.
H3527.portee: This word reminds the reader that quantity never replaces quality. Multiplying words does not guarantee being heard or being right. It invites sobriety in speech: to say little and well, rather than much and without wisdom. For the believer, it is a lesson on discernment: accumulating is not building.

sens: What has happened before the present moment
What took place long ago, in a distant past
What returns, repeats endlessly over time
H3528.detail:
1. The word denotes what has occurred before now: "What is has already been" (Ecclesiastes 3:15), meaning that everything we see today has existed before us. It is the simple idea of anteriority.
2. It can also refer to a very ancient past, "long ago": the memory of the wise as well as that of the fool quickly fades, for "already the days that follow, all is forgotten" (Ecclesiastes 2:16), suggesting that forgetfulness quickly catches up with us in the course of time.
3. The word highlights the repetition of things: "If there is a thing of which one says: Look at this, it is new! this thing has already existed in the centuries that preceded us" (Ecclesiastes 1:10), showing that nothing truly new appears — everything has already happened.
H3528.origine: The Hebrew word כְּבָר (kebar) comes from a root meaning "to finish" or "to accomplish." Its primary sense is that of something completed, accomplished, hence the idea that it is from the past, from what is bygone. It is an ancient adverb in Hebrew, frequently used in biblical texts to mark the time that has passed.
H3528.emploi: This adverb appears 8 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in Ecclesiastes (6 times out of the 8 occurrences provided). There, it expresses the philosophical weariness of Qoheleth in the face of human history: everything that exists has already existed, everything that is done has already been done. Ecclesiastes uses it to show the vanity of the search for novelty (1:10), the monotonous repetition of history (3:15), and even the equality of the dead who are "already dead" — a paradoxical expression to say that death makes all the dead alike (4:2). It is a word of pessimism or realism in the face of the cycle of things.
H3528.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize that he is not the first to confront questions of meaning, death, and vanity: Qoheleth posed them before him, and they are ancient. It also reminds us that God will never be surprised: everything that happens, He has already seen. But more fundamentally, it pushes us to seek what does not pass, beyond the repetitive cycle of the world.

sens: River of Babylon where the Israelite exiles settled
H3529.detail: 1. Kebar is a river located in Babylon (the region of present-day Iraq). It is near this watercourse that the Israelites deported by Nebuchadnezzar settled after the fall of Jerusalem. The prophet Ezekiel, who lived among these exiles, received his visions near the Kebar River: "as I was among the captives by the river of Kebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God" (Ezekiel 1:1). Thus, it is the setting for Ezekiel's prophetic ministry, the place where God manifested Himself to him and where he heard the call to prophesy.
H3529.origine: The name Kebar literally means "far" or "distant" in Akkadian (the language of the Babylonians): it evokes the remoteness of this place. Historians often identify Kebar with the royal canal of Babylon, possibly the Habor (an irrigation canal connected to the Euphrates). It was an important site in the region where authorities settled deported populations.
H3529.emploi: Kebar appears exclusively in the book of Ezekiel, in six verses (Ezekiel 1:1, 1:3, 3:15, 3:23, 10:15, 10:20, 10:22, 43:3). It is always referred to as "the river of Kebar" or "by the river of Kebar." It is there that Ezekiel receives his great visions: the cherubim and the chariot-throne of God (chapters 1 and 10), and later the glory of the Lord returning to the restored temple (43:3). Kebar is the geographical and spiritual place where the prophetic ministry of the prophet is exercised among the exiles.
H3529.portee: Kebar reminds us that God does not isolate Himself when His people are in exile and distress. It is in a foreign land, far from the temple of Jerusalem, that the Lord manifests Himself to Ezekiel and equips him with His word to encourage the captives. The river of Kebar thus becomes the sign that God's presence and grace follow His people beyond borders, even in the darkest moments of their history.

sens: space that separates two points or places
distance to be covered on a road
H3530.detail:
