1. The word denotes the spatial interval between two places: Genesis 35:16 mentions "a certain distance" between Bethel and Ephrath, meaning the space to be crossed between these two cities. This is the most concrete and geographical meaning of the term.
2. It can also evoke the journey itself, the portion of the way that must be traveled: in Genesis 48:7, Jacob speaks of the distance where Rachel died "on the way to Ephrath," thus emphasizing the route taken. In 2 Kings 5:19, when Naaman distances himself from Elisha "at a certain distance," it also shows the space he puts between himself and the prophet as he departs.
H3530.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of gap or separation. It is related to other Hebrew words meaning "far" or "to distance oneself." It is a concrete and geographical term, without particular moral or theological connotation.
H3530.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in narrative prose. It is used to describe journeys or intervals between places in biographical contexts (the movements of Jacob and Rachel, Naaman's healing). Each time, it emphasizes the existence of a space to be crossed or a spatial separation, without dramatization: it simply notes a distance traveled or to be traveled.
H3530.portee: This word reminds us of the concrete reality of biblical journeys: characters do not move instantaneously, but must cover distances, spend time on the roads, and accept the separations imposed by space. For the reader, it is a detail that anchors the narratives in real life and shows how divine providence accompanies people in their earthly journeys, even in the midst of trials — like the death of Rachel that occurred on the way.

sens: Kitchen or agricultural utensil used to separate fine grains from coarse grains or impurities
In a figurative sense: the action of sifting, shaking to sort
That which tests, separates, distinguishes
H3531.detail:
1. A sieve is a utensil made of a cloth or mesh stretched over a frame, used to sift flour, grains, or other materials to remove foreign bodies or separate different sizes. It was a common household tool in Israel during the time of the prophets (Amos 9:9).
2. The verb to sift refers to the action of passing something through a sieve, shaking it vigorously. When one shakes a sieve, the small grains and dust escape through the mesh, while the larger grains remain on the surface, allowing for effective sorting.
3. The Bible uses the image of the sieve in a figurative sense to describe a trial that reveals the true nature of things or people: God shakes Israel among the nations to separate the superficial from the lasting, the unbeliever from the authentic believer.
H3531.origine: The Hebrew word כְּבָרָה (ke.va.rah) comes from a root meaning "to sift" or "to sift through." In ancient Israel, it was an essential utensil for the home and harvest. The image of the sieve is common in the ancient Near East to evoke sorting, separation, and testing.
H3531.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew New Testament and in the Greek text of the Septuagint: in Amos 9:9. The prophet Amos uses it in a word of judgment and hope: God announces that He will "sift" the house of Israel among all the peoples, in order to punish the guilty but also to preserve a faithful remnant. This image emphasizes that God will not destroy indiscriminately, but will perform a sorting: the sinners will fall, but "only one grain" — the faithful remnant — will not fall to the ground. The sieve reveals what has value and what must be rejected.
H3531.portee: This image of the sieve reminds the believer that trials are not in vain: they reveal the quality of faith and the sincerity of the heart. Just as the authentic grain does not fall when it is sifted, the true believer remains stable under trial. It is a source of comfort for those going through difficulties: these are a means by which God separates the superficial from the lasting, not to destroy, but to purify.

sens: Young sheep, generally male, in its first year
Animal offered as a sacrifice to the Lord in temple rituals
Innocent and vulnerable creature, image of gentleness and submission
H3532.detail:
1. A lamb is a young sheep, typically a male under one year old. It is a domesticated animal raised in flocks. The Bible often mentions "a year-old lamb without defect" for sacrifices, as in Exodus 12:5 where the people choose a lamb for Passover: the animal must be young, healthy, and suitable for offering.

2. In Israelite worship, the lamb occupies a central place: it was offered daily as a perpetual burnt offering (Numbers 28:3), during major festivals (Numbers 28:19, Numbers 29:13), and for guilt or sin offerings (Leviticus 4:32). These offerings express communion with God and acknowledgment of His goodness. The lamb, a precious and useful animal, represents a true gift of the heart.

3. By its nature — small, gentle, unable to defend itself — the lamb becomes the biblical image of innocence and vulnerability. This is why Jesus is called "the Lamb of God": like a lamb led to the slaughter without protest, He accepts to die for the sins of the world.
H3532.origine: The Hebrew word keves comes from a root that evokes the idea of youth and contained strength. It specifically designates the young animal, distinct from the adult ram (ayil) and the ewe (kibsa). The family of the word includes terms related to sheep in all its forms. In the Greek Old Testament, this word is often translated as "amnos" (ἀμνός), which in the New Testament takes on a profound spiritual dimension with the image of the Passover and redemptive Lamb.
H3532.emploi: The word lamb appears more than a hundred times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the books of the Law and Numbers. It is absent from poetry and the major prophets. Its use is rigorously ritual and calendrical: every day, two unblemished lambs must be burned as a burnt offering (Numbers 28:3-4); at each major festival of the people (Passover, Pentecost, Sukkot), lambs are offered in increasing numbers (Numbers 28-29); for individual sacrifices, a lamb is presented when a vow or purification requires it (Leviticus 12:6, Numbers 6:12). The word does not vary in meaning: it is always the animal destined for the altar, symbol of regular worship and the covenant between Israel and its God.
H3532.portee: For the believer, meditating on the biblical lamb illuminates the meaning of Christ's sacrifice. Jesus, called "the Lamb of God" in the Gospel of John, encompasses all the associations of the Old Testament lamb: He is the Innocent offered for all, the Perpetual Gift that reconciles us with God, the fulfillment of all ancient sacrifices. Understanding what a lamb was in Jewish worship helps us grasp the depth of this title: Jesus is not just a victim, but the awaited Lamb, the one in whom the promise of redemption is fulfilled.

sens: To subject someone or something to one's authority, to make them subordinate
To defeat an enemy or a people by force
To violate or do violence to someone, to dominate against their will
To tame or master (an animal or a natural force)
H3533.detail:
1. To subject someone or something to one's authority means to make them subordinate, someone or something that obeys. It is to place under one's power in a lasting way. In Genesis 1:28, God tells humans: "subdue" the earth, meaning to master it and make good use of it.
2. To defeat an enemy or a people by force means to reduce them to helplessness through battle or military domination. In 2 Samuel 8:11, David dedicates the gold taken from the nations he had "defeated" — he had subdued them through war.
3. To violate or do violence to someone means to dominate them brutally and against their will, taking away their consent or freedom. In Esther 7:8, the king asks in horror if Haman dared to "do violence" to the queen in his house — this is an unjust and criminal domination.
4. To tame or master a natural force means to make it obedient and harmless. This can apply to animals or elements that humans must learn to control.
H3533.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּבַשׁ (kavash) comes from a root expressing the idea of treading, walking on, crushing underfoot. The primary image is that of physical domination — the one who treads underfoot masters what is beneath. This root also gives the name "rider" (one who rides a horse and dominates their mount). The word thus describes a subjugation obtained by force or the exercise of power.
H3533.emploi: The verb כָּבַשׁ appears 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the sense of "to subdue" and "to conquer." In Genesis 1:28, it refers to a positive mission: humans are to subdue the earth to use it wisely. But the military and political context often recurs: Numbers 32:29 speaks of lands "subdued" after victory; 2 Samuel 8:11 mentions the nations "defeated" by David. The word takes on a darker hue in Jeremiah 34:16, where freed slaves are forcibly "made to return" to servitude — subjugation becomes unjust and guilty. In Esther 7:8, it is an attempt to "do violence" against the queen. The verb thus describes both military victory and personal oppression or violence.
H3533.portee: This word reminds Christians of two calls from the Lord. First, in Genesis 1:28, the vocation to "subdue" the earth is not a permission to exploit it selfishly, but a duty of responsible stewardship and management of creation. Secondly, the accounts of subjugation and violence show the abuses of human power: when one unjustly "submits," they violate God's plan for the dignity of each person. The Christian is called to exercise authority with justice, never with cruel domination.

sens: Elevated surface on which one places their feet to access a seat
Base or support placed in front of a throne or piece of furniture
Symbol of domination and power
Humble support that honors the one who rests upon it
H3534.detail:
1. A footstool is a small platform or low stool placed in front of a seat — a throne, a high chair — so that the one who ascends can place their feet on it and access the seat easily. In 2 Chronicles 9:18, King Solomon's royal throne was accompanied by a golden footstool, a prestigious object that facilitated access to the royal seat while highlighting its height and importance.
2. In the Hebrew Old Testament, the footstool is not just a practical object: it often designates what rests upon the power of a king or what he dominates. It is a royal accessory that embodies honor and majesty.
3. The word can also express domination: the one who places their feet on something masters it. This is why this term, in the Bible, sometimes symbolizes the submission of what is under the feet — enemies, subjugated peoples — to the one who reigns.
H3534.origine: The Hebrew word כֶּבֶשׁ (kevesh) comes from a root that means "to tread, to trample, to subdue." The footstool is literally what is trodden underfoot. It is a concrete word, directly related to the action of walking and dominating. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often corresponds to ὑποπόδιον (hypopodion), which conveys the same idea: the footrest, the pedestal.
H3534.emploi: This word appears only once in the translations of the Segond, in 2 Chronicles 9:18, where it describes Solomon's golden footstool. Although infrequent in this exact form, the concept of the footstool — what serves as a base and what is trodden — is omnipresent in the Hebrew Bible: it symbolizes the support of power, the voluntary or forced lowering of the one who is underfoot, and the honor of the one who places their feet upon it. The royal context of its unique use bears witness to this: it is an object that embodies the splendor and majesty of Solomon's reign.
H3534.portee: The footstool of Solomon's throne reminds us that true royal power is accompanied by precise details and staging: each element of the throne — its steps, its golden footstool, its carved lions — contributes to manifesting the authority and glory of the king. For the Christian reader, this detail invites meditation on the contrast between earthly thrones, so richly adorned, and the throne of the Lord, infinitely higher and more glorious. It is also an opportunity to see how the Bible honors royalty according to the Old Covenant, while opening the heart to the eternal King of the New Testament.

sens: Young female sheep
Animal offered as a sacrifice in the worship of Israel
Symbol of gentleness, innocence, and vulnerability
H3535.detail:
1. The sheep is a young female of the sheep, a valuable livestock animal in Palestine. It provides wool, milk, and meat. Abraham sets aside seven to seal an agreement with Abimelech (Genesis 21:28), showing that a sheep had real commercial value and could serve as currency or collateral.
2. In worship, a one-year-old unblemished sheep is a common sacrificial animal: it was offered as a sin offering or in thanksgiving, as shown in the ordinance of the nazirite (Numbers 6:14) or the purification of the leper (Leviticus 14:10). This religious status emphasizes that it was deemed acceptable before God.
3. The parable of the poor man and his sheep (2 Samuel 12:3-4) reveals the emotional dimension: the animal is cherished, treated like a child, sleeping on the master's chest. This image of wounded innocence reinforces the crime of the rich man who steals it — David is so moved that he pronounces his own condemnation.
H3535.origine: The Hebrew word kívshah comes from the root that expresses the idea of virility or sexual maturity applied to the female. In Hebrew, one distinguishes the ram (ayil), the male sheep, and the ewe (kívshah), the female of reproductive age. This precision reflects the economic importance of the flock: each animal, according to its sex and age, had a defined place and value in the pastoral economy of Israel.
H3535.emploi: The word kívshah appears 8 times, mainly in legal and cultic contexts. In Genesis 21, Abraham uses it to seal a covenant: the commercial act underscores his authority and wealth. In Leviticus and Numbers, it is prescribed as a sacrificial victim, always without blemish, showing the requirement of ritual purity. But the most memorable use is in 2 Samuel 12, where Nathan tells David the story of the poor man and his beloved sheep: here, the animal becomes the pathetic symbol of innocence stolen by the powerful, awakening the king's conscience.
H3535.portee: The sheep reveals both the economic and religious structure of Israel, but also the injustice that weighs on the weak. It teaches that even a small animal, the possession of one who has nothing, is worthy of respect and love. For the Christian reader, the image of the innocent and precious sheep paves the way for understanding Jesus, the shepherd and lamb — the one who gives himself for the lost and the weak.

sens: Large very hot oven, used for firing pottery or melting metals
Place or instrument producing intense heat and a lot of smoke
Image of violent destruction and divine anger
H3536.detail:
1. A furnace is a large industrial oven, like those used by potters or blacksmiths to fire clay or melt metal at very high temperatures. It is a functional piece of equipment, ordinary in antiquity, but impressive due to its intense heat.
2. By extension, the word designates anything that produces extreme and visible heat and smoke: the furnace can be literal (an oven) or compared to a natural phenomenon. When Abraham looks at Sodom (Genesis 19:28), the destruction resembles "the smoke of a furnace"—a thick column of smoke rising from the ground.
3. In texts that speak of divine anger, the furnace becomes an image of judgment and punishment. In Exodus, Moses throws furnace ash into the air (Exodus 9:8-10), and this ash causes sores on the Egyptians: the furnace is the instrument of the plague. At Sinai (Exodus 19:18), the mountain smokes like a furnace because the Lord descends in the midst of fire—this is the terrifying manifestation of His presence and power.
H3536.origine: The Hebrew word kiv.shan likely comes from a root meaning the action of burning or heating intensely. It may be related to cognate terms in other Semitic languages for oven or furnace. It is a fairly simple word that describes a well-known technical object to all the peoples of the ancient Levant: every village had its potters and blacksmiths with their furnaces.
H3536.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, only in the Pentateuch (Genesis and Exodus). It is always accompanied by the mention of smoke: this detail emphasizes the intensity of the phenomenon. In Genesis 19:28, it is used to describe the destruction of Sodom; in the two passages of Exodus 9, it evokes the instrument of judgment on Egypt (the furnace ash that causes the plagues); in Exodus 19:18, it represents the theophany, the descent of the Lord enveloped in fire. Each use reinforces the idea of divine power exercised through fire and heat.
H3536.portee: For the Christian reader, the furnace in these texts is never neutral: it speaks of God's judgment on sin and the manifestation of His power. Sodom smoking like a furnace, the ash striking Egypt, the burning Sinai—these are not images of gentleness, but of irresistible divine justice. It is a call to respect the holiness of God and to take His judgment seriously.

sens: Ceramic or pottery container, medium to large in size, carried by hand or on the shoulder
Vessel used to draw water from a spring or well
Fragile container, symbol of human fragility
H3537.detail:
1. A pitcher is a clay pot, large and sturdy enough to hold liquid, especially water. It is easily carried by hand or balanced on the shoulder. Rebekah fills her pitcher at the spring (Genesis 24:16), and the widow of Zarephath draws water for Elijah (1 Kings 17:12).
2. The pitcher is the daily tool of women for fetching water. It is an act of service and hospitality: giving a drink to the traveler also means offering him the pitcher or watering him from it (Genesis 24:18, Genesis 24:46).
3. Because it is fragile and breaks easily, the pitcher becomes a biblical image of human fragility. Gideon and his men break their pitchers to let the light of the torches shine through (Judges 7:19), and this fragility manifests man's dependence on God.
H3537.origine: The Hebrew word kad designates an everyday object: a portable container made of clay. Its etymology refers to the idea of capacity, of holding. The pitcher is an ancient and universal utensil in the Middle East, essential in a home without running water. This term also appears in Aramaic and other Semitic languages with the same meaning.
H3537.emploi: The word kad appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Old Testament. It is very present in the story of Rebekah (Genesis 24), where the pitcher symbolizes the humble service of the young girl towards Abraham's servant. It is also found in the story of Gideon (Judges 7), who breaks the pitchers to let the torches shine and achieve a miraculous victory. It appears again with the widow of Zarephath who draws water for the prophet Elijah (1 Kings 17). These narratives show both the ordinary domestic use and the symbolic role of the fragile vessel in God's plan.
H3537.portee: The pitcher invites us to meditate on our fragility: we are, like it, fragile clay vessels, dependent on God. It also teaches us simple hospitality and service: welcoming the thirsty traveler means offering him water with humility, like Rebekah. Finally, the breaking of the pitchers by Gideon reminds us that it is God, not our strength, who wins the victory: our weakness becomes strength when we rely on Him.

sens: Word contrary to truth
Statement intended to deceive
H3538.detail:
1. A lie is a word that contradicts the truth, a false statement presented as true. In Daniel 2:9, King Nebuchadnezzar fears that the magicians will tell him lies instead of truly revealing the dream he had.
2. More broadly, it is any statement that seeks to deceive or mislead: a falsehood spoken knowingly to mislead the listener. The context of the forgotten dream shows that the king specifically rejects this trickery—he wants the raw truth, not words intended to dupe him.
H3538.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of deception and disappointment. It belongs to the family of terms designating falsehood and lies, which often appear in the Bible to describe what opposes God's faithfulness and honesty.
H3538.emploi: This word appears only once in the preserved Hebrew text, in Daniel 2:9. King Nebuchadnezzar, faced with the enigma of a forgotten dream, fears that his advisors will serve him lies rather than provide the authentic interpretation. The usage emphasizes the contrast between human deception and the divine truth he ultimately seeks—truth that only Daniel can reveal by the Spirit of God.
H3538.portee: This word reminds us that a lie is a weapon of deception and that God is the God of truth and faithfulness. In the face of the world's tricks and lies, the believer can trust in the One who never lies and who calls for honesty of heart.

sens: Precious stone of intense red color
Object of luxury and wealth in trade
Ornament of splendor and heavenly beauty
H3539.detail: 1. The ruby is a precious stone of brilliant red, very rare and very expensive. It is a noble mineral, valued in antiquity as it is today. 2. In the provided biblical passages, the ruby is among the goods of great price: Syria trades in it, which shows its status as a precious and sought-after item (Ezekiel 27:16). 3. In prophetic vision, the ruby becomes an element of beauty and glory: the battlements of the restored Jerusalem will be made of rubies, evoking a heavenly splendor and divine magnificence (Isaiah 54:12). The ruby symbolizes here the magnificence of the new world promised by God.
H3539.origine: The Hebrew word kad.kod designates this gemstone since antiquity. Its exact etymology remains uncertain, but it can refer to the ruby or related red precious stones. The term is rare in biblical Hebrew (only two occurrences), which shows the importance and unique value attributed to this stone. In ancient Near Eastern texts, the ruby was one of the most prized stones alongside lapis lazuli and gold.
H3539.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always as a precious stone of great price. In Ezekiel 27:16, the ruby is a trade commodity between Syria and Tyre, listed among other luxury goods (purple, embroidery, coral). In Isaiah 54:12, it takes on a prophetic and symbolic dimension: the battlements of Jerusalem will be adorned with rubies in the vision of eschatological restoration. This rarity underscores the theological importance: the ruby is mentioned only to magnify either earthly wealth or the promised heavenly glory.
H3539.portee: The ruby reminds the reader that God wants to restore His people in a brilliant and lasting magnificence. This vision of a Jerusalem adorned with precious stones is not a promise of material wealth, but the assurance that the glory of God will completely transform His dwelling and His people. It is a comfort addressed to Israel in exile: beyond the present destruction, God will build something more beautiful, more splendid than ever.

sens: King of Elam who dominated several kingdoms of Canaan during the time of the Patriarchs
Enemy defeated by Abraham during a coalition of kings' war
H3540.detail:
1. Kedorlaomer was a powerful king of Elam (a kingdom located to the east, in present-day Persia) who exerted his authority over the kings of Canaan. For twelve years, the Canaanite kings paid him tribute and obeyed him (Genesis 14:4), which shows his political and military control over the region.
2. In the thirteenth year, the vassal kings revolted against his yoke. Kedorlaomer responded by organizing a military campaign with three other allied kings, achieving victories against several peoples such as the Rephaim and the Emim (Genesis 14:5). Abraham then intervened to rescue his nephew Lot, defeating Kedorlaomer and his allies (Genesis 14:17), which reversed the balance of power in the region.
H3540.origine: The Hebrew name "Kedorlaomer" literally means "bundle of sheaves," composed of the Hebrew "kedor" (bundle) and "la" (of) and "omer" (sheaf). It is a foreign name adapted to Hebrew, reflecting the Mesopotamian origin of this historical figure.
H3540.emploi: Kedorlaomer appears only in Genesis 14, the account of a coalition of four eastern kings who invaded Canaan. The chapter designates him as the main adversary (Genesis 14:1), the suzerain to whom the local kings had submitted (Genesis 14:4), the leader of the victorious military campaign (Genesis 14:5), and finally the king whom Abraham defeated in battle (Genesis 14:9 and 14:17). His role illustrates both the power of eastern empires and the vulnerability of Canaanite kingdoms, but also Abraham's ability to effectively intervene in the geopolitical affairs of his time.
H3540.portee: The account of Kedorlaomer reveals that Abraham was not a mere passive nomad, but a man capable of organizing a military force and achieving victory. This victory over an otherwise powerful king demonstrates that God's promise to Abraham of a numerous offspring and land also includes concrete protection and authority. It is an encouragement: God's call can make us more than conquerors, even in the face of seemingly superior forces.

sens: In this manner, in this way
At this moment, at this precise moment
Up to this moment, until now
Behold, look
H3541.detail:
1. « In this manner, in this way »: the word indicates how an action is performed or how things are. It is the quintessential word for reporting the word of God: « Thus says the Lord » introduces a prophetic message (1 Kings 21:19; Isaiah 45:18; Ezekiel 3:11). Thus also commands: « Thus you shall do » means « in that manner, obey my instructions ».
2. « At this moment, at this precise moment »: the word situates in the present or immediate time. In Genesis 22:5, Abraham tells his servants « Stay here », marking the moment when he separates from them.
3. « Up to this moment, until now »: expresses continuity from the past to the present. In 1 Samuel 9:9, « until now » shows what has always been practiced.
4. « Behold, look »: reinforces an invitation to observe or pay attention. In Genesis 15:5, « Look toward heaven » is accompanied by this particle to point out the object to contemplate.
H3541.origine: The word comes from a very ancient Hebrew root expressing the idea of being here, being there, and thus in this manner. It is a primitive adverb used to direct attention to something or to situate a moment, an action. The Aramaic form כָּה (kah) is almost identical and carries the same meaning. This word belongs to the oldest core of the Hebrew language.
H3541.emploi: Used more than 540 times in the Hebrew Bible, « thus » is one of the most frequent adverbs. It predominates especially in prophetic speeches, where « Thus says the Lord » becomes a stereotypical formula to authenticate a divine message (1 Kings 21:19, Jeremiah 26:18, Ezekiel 32:11). It is also found in narratives to describe how things are done (Exodus 32:27, Joshua 6:3), in divine orders (Numbers 6:23, Deuteronomy 7:5), and in everyday conversation to affirm, confirm, or point something out solemnly (Ruth 1:17, 1 Samuel 14:44). Its meaning remains stable: it always marks certainty, precision, authority.
H3541.portee: This simple yet powerful word reminds us that the word of God is not vague or ambiguous, but precise and effective. « Thus says the Lord » asserts that God speaks directly, clearly, to men, and that His instructions have absolute significance. For the Christian reader, this underscores the importance of obedience: God does not say « maybe », He says « thus ». It is also an invitation to clarity in communication and faithfulness.

sens: at this point in the narrative, at this place in the text
up to now, until then
H3542.detail:
1. The word designates the point where one is in a narrative or enumeration. In Daniel 7:28, « Here ended the words » means that it is at this place, at this point in the text, that the vision Daniel has just reported concludes — one could say « it is here that » or « it is at this point ».
2. It can also mark a limit in time or progression: « up to here » or « until then ». It conveys the idea of « until now », of everything that has elapsed up to the moment being discussed.
H3542.origine: This Aramaic word (the language Daniel speaks in this section of the book) corresponds to the Hebrew koh (כֹּה), which means « thus » or « in this manner ». The two words are close in meaning and root. In biblical Aramaic, kah is used to mark a stopping point or a key moment in the discourse.
H3542.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:28. Daniel reports his vision of the four beasts, and at the end of this long mysterious discourse, he writes: « Here ended the words. » It is a pivotal moment: the vision stops there, and Daniel turns to his personal reactions (he is troubled, he changes color, he meditates). The word thus marks the end of a section and the pivot of the narrative.
H3542.portee: This small word reminds us that God structures history and time through stages. For Daniel as for us, there are moments when God speaks, then stops — and it is up to us to receive what He has said and keep it in our hearts, as Daniel does. It is an invitation to listen attentively and meditate on God's words at the decisive points of our lives.

sens: to lose its brightness, to become pale or dull
to lose strength, to weaken physically
to lose courage, to become discouraged
to become obscure, dark, indistinct
H3543A.detail:
1. The word first describes a visible loss of brightness: a color that fades, a light that goes out. In Leviticus 13:6, the leprous sore is examined: if it has become « pale » after washing, it means it has diminished and the man is declared clean. It is the image of a hue that fades away.
2. In a physical sense, the verb denotes the weakening of the body. When Moses dies at 120 years, his eye was not « weakened » (Deuteronomy 34:7): his sight was still good, his body had not lost its vigor. The word paints the inevitable decline of strength with age.
3. On an emotional and moral level, to weaken means to lose confidence or courage. In Isaiah 42:4, the Servant of the Lord will not « become discouraged »: he will not give up his mission despite obstacles. The verb then expresses a relaxation of determination.
4. Finally, the word can evoke the darkness that veils: Job says that his eye is « darkened » by pain (Job 17:7), as if sorrow tarnished his vision. It is a kind of inner dimming.
H3543A.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that expresses the idea of becoming weak, pale, or obscure. The simple form (Qal) describes a natural process — something that loses its intensity, its color, or its strength — while the intensive form (Piel) reinforces this meaning, emphasizing the action of making weak or allowing to weaken. The word can evoke both physical discoloration (a stain that fades) and moral exhaustion or loss of energy.
H3543A.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the Old Testament, mainly in legal passages, historical narratives, and poetry. In Leviticus (13:6, 13:56), it is used in the diagnosis of skin diseases: a lesion that « pales » is a good sign. In Deuteronomy 34:7, it characterizes Moses' vigor at his death, where the verb is negated to show the patriarch's exceptional strength. In prophetic and poetic texts (Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Zechariah), the meaning broadens: it denotes discouragement, moral exhaustion, or numbness in the face of trials. In Isaiah 42:4, the context of the suffering Servant emphasizes unwavering determination — it will never weaken. The word thus navigates between the concrete (loss of color, fatigue of the body) and the abstract (morality, tenacity).
H3543A.portee: This word reminds the reader that weakness is human and often inevitable — pain, doubt, fatigue threaten everyone. But it also invites perseverance: the Servant in Isaiah refuses to weaken despite his sufferings, a model for the believer in trial. The verb invites not to be discouraged, to maintain a lively trust in God even when everything seems to darken.

sens: To treat someone or something with contempt, to judge them unworthy
To render despicable, to cover with shame
To neglect, to let things happen without intervening
H3543B.detail:
1. To treat someone or something with contempt: this means to look down on them, to judge them unworthy of consideration or respect. In 1 Samuel 3:13, the sons of the priest Eli "made themselves despicable" by their crimes, meaning they acted in such a serious manner that God judged them unworthy of honor.
2. To render despicable: this means to give a shameful reputation, to cover with dishonor. When one despises someone, they publicly belittle them and disavow them.
3. To neglect to correct or reprimand: this means to turn a blind eye to evil, to let things happen without intervening. Eli did not reprimand his sons for their detestable acts, which contributed to their disgrace.
H3543B.origine: The Hebrew verb כָּהָה (kahah) carries the idea of diminishment and loss of value. It is related to the image of something that weakens, losing its luster or dignity. The word evokes both moral judgment (to consider as worthless) and social effect (to be dishonored or belittled).
H3543B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Samuel 3:13, in a context of serious divine reproach. The prophet Samuel announces to the priest Eli that God will eternally punish his house because his sons have committed abominable acts and Eli did not reprimand them. The term describes both the unworthiness of the sons (who "made themselves despicable") and the father's culpable inaction. It is a rare but very meaningful word: it marks the rupture between God and Eli's priestly house.
H3543B.portee: This word reminds the believer that God judges severely the deliberate contempt of His law and the absence of correction in the face of evil. It also speaks to parents and leaders: allowing sin to go unaddressed increases guilt and attracts divine judgment. It is a warning against moral passivity.

sens: Having a weakened, dull, or whitish color
(for sight) Not clear, troubled, obscured
(for a light) Weakening or disappearing
Losing its luster or strength
H3544.detail: 1. When speaking of a spot or eruption on the skin, this word denotes a hue that lacks the intensity or relief of a true lesion: the spot remains on the surface, without sinking into the flesh. This is what the priest looks for in cases of leprosy (Leviticus 13:21) — a pale spot indicates healing or a minor condition. 2. Sight can be pale or "troubled": this refers to weakened vision, as in Eli, the old priest whose eyes no longer see clearly (1 Samuel 3:2). 3. A wick or light is pale when it weakens, no longer shining as before: Isaiah 42:3 speaks of a wick that still burns but gradually goes out, an image of the Lord's tenderness for those who are fragile. 4. Figuratively, pale suggests a loss of luster or strength — the weakening of a presence or life.
H3544.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes darkness and weakening. Its fundamental image is that of something becoming blurred, losing its clarity or brightness — like a color fading or a light dimming. The family includes words related to darkness and the depression of the heart.
H3544.emploi: The word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Leviticus (six occurrences) in the laws concerning leprosy. It is used to describe the appearance of a skin lesion: when it is pale, it is a good sign — it indicates that it does not have the depth or severity of declared leprosy. The priest must examine whether the spot is pale or, on the contrary, sunken. Once, in the prophet Isaiah, the word applies to a wick that is going out: it then becomes a beautiful image of discretion and compassion.
H3544.portee: This word invites the reader to look at reality with nuance. A pale spot, less visible, is not necessarily serious: it is also a lesson about healing and hope. The image of the wick going out in Isaiah reveals the tenderness of the Messiah — He does not destroy what is weak, but protects it. For the Christian, this word speaks of how God treats the fragile: not with brutality, but with vigilant gentleness.

sens: That which relieves or heals a wound, an injury
That which soothes or diminishes suffering
That which repairs or restores what is damaged
H3545.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to that which heals a physical wound or injury. In Nahum 3:19, the prophet says to Nineveh: "There is no remedy for your wound," meaning that its injury is so grave, so deep that no treatment can heal it.
2. More broadly, it refers to that which calms, which diminishes any pain or suffering. The image is that of a wound to which an ointment or balm is applied to soothe it.
3. The word also evokes the idea of restoration: a remedy puts back in order what is broken or damaged. That is why it can mean "relief" in a broad sense, as if returning to balance after an affliction.
H3545.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to become weak," "to weaken," or "to become soft." From this derives the idea of "diminishing" the intensity of a pain, "weakening" it until it is healed. The word belongs to the family of terms that express soothing and the end of tension.
H3545.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nahum 3:19. It is found in the context of God's judgment against Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. The prophet announces that the city will be defeated irreversibly: its destruction is so complete that there is no remedy, no treatment, no means of restoring it. It is a word of absolute condemnation.
H3545.portee: This verse reminds us that some consequences of sin can be irreversible and definitive. Nineveh, which has rejected God and oppressed the peoples, has no escape: there is no remedy for its condition. For the believer, this word invites us to take seriously the gravity of God's judgment and the importance of turning to Him before it is too late. It is also an invitation to seek from God the true remedy for our spiritual wounds.

sens: To have the capacity, strength, or ability to do something
To be able to successfully perform an action
To have the necessary means to accomplish a task
H3546.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses the material or intellectual capacity to do something. In a concrete sense, it means having the required strength or skills. When the wise men of Babylon cannot read the writing on the wall (Daniel 5:8), it is simply because they lack the ability to do so — their intelligence or knowledge does not apply.

2. It can also denote the ability to successfully accomplish a specific action. Belshazzar (Daniel) can provide the interpretation of the dream (Daniel 4:18) because he possesses the spirit of the holy gods, meaning a supernatural ability. The word then emphasizes not just theoretical possibility, but effective and recognized capacity.

3. In context, the term often marks a distinction between those who can and those who cannot — a question of ability that determines success or failure. Here, the ordinary scholars are powerless, while Daniel alone possesses the necessary power.
H3546.origine: The Aramaic verb כְּהַל (ke.hal) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to have the strength to" or "to be strong for." It is not a passive possession, but the expression of an active and operative capacity. The word is used in late Aramaic, particularly in the book of Daniel, where it denotes the faculty to accomplish what one undertakes.
H3546.emploi: This verb appears only four times in the Bible, exclusively in the book of Daniel (chapters 2, 4, and 5). It is used each time to express the capacity or incapacity of the Babylonian sages in the face of divine mysteries: Nebuchadnezzar's dream (2:26), its interpretation (4:18), and the reading of the mysterious writing on the wall (5:8, 5:15). Its systematic use creates a dramatic contrast — the magicians, astrologers, and wise men of the king repeatedly fail, while Daniel, inspired by the Spirit of God, alone possesses the ability to succeed. The word thus emphasizes the supremacy of divine wisdom over human wisdom.
H3546.portee: This word reminds us that true capacity — the one that truly matters — does not come from human intelligence alone, but from God. The wise of this world, even the most prestigious, are powerless in the face of God's mysteries until God himself grants them understanding. For the believer, this invites recognition that our power to act and understand the things of God entirely depends on His grace and His Spirit.

sens: To perform the functions and service of a priest
To be consecrated and clothed with priestly dignity
To conduct worship and intercession before God for the people
H3547.detail:
1. This verb describes the concrete action of the priest in the service of the sanctuary: offering sacrifices, wearing sacred garments, performing all the rites instituted by God. When Eleazar and Ithamar "exercised the priesthood" after the death of Nadab and Abihu (Numbers 3:4), they took charge of all this solemn religious work before the altar.
2. The word also designates the accession to this office, the consecration itself. When Aaron and his sons are "consecrated" to "be in my service in the priesthood" (Exodus 28:1, 28:41), it refers to the anointing that clothes them with this authority and holy responsibility.
3. The priesthood includes spiritual mediation: the priest stands before God for the entire nation, thus ensuring the link between the people and their Creator. It is a function of representation and intercession, not just a technical job.
H3547.origine: This verb comes from the Hebrew root that gives "kohèn" (priest). The original image is that of service, access to the sanctuary. The family of the word includes the term "priesthood" itself. In Hebrew, the verb in the causative form (Piel) intensifies the idea: one does not simply perform service, one actively and regularly fulfills the priestly function. This root appears throughout all periods of biblical history.
H3547.emploi: This verb appears 23 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of the Law (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in Chronicles. It is used to recount the original consecration of Aaron and his sons, and then to describe the ongoing service of the priest in the sanctuary. The Segond translates it as "priesthood" (noun), "service", "to exercise the priesthood" or "priestly function". After the return from exile, the word also applies to the Levites who take on this role (Ezekiel 44:13). A notable nuance: the verb is never used for acts of illegitimate or profane worship, unlike other verbs of religious action.
H3547.portee: Understanding this word helps to grasp the holiness of Israelite worship: the priesthood was not a personal honor, but a service owed to God, required by divine institution and consecration. For the Christian, this sheds light on the Epistle to the Hebrews, which shows that Christ is the ultimate High Priest: He "exercises the priesthood" once for all, and all believers become a "royal priesthood" (1 Peter 2:9). The word reminds us that access to God requires mediation and holiness.

sens: One who offers sacrifices to the God of Israel in the temple
One who fulfills religious and ritual functions in Israel's worship
Minister of worship of a foreign religion
Leader or authority in a religious community
H3548.detail:
1. The priest is primarily one who presents offerings to the Lord — this is his most visible function. Leviticus constantly describes the priest receiving an animal, examining it, placing it on the altar, and burning the prescribed parts (Leviticus 1:5-17; Leviticus 4:3-31). It is a very precise ritual act, regulated by the law.
2. The priest also performs broader religious functions: inspecting the house to recognize leprosy (Leviticus 13:2-8), purifying the faithful, declaring what is clean or unclean. He is a religious expert, not just an officiant.
3. The word also applies to priests of foreign religions: Egyptian priests (Genesis 41:45), or Melchizedek who offers bread and wine to the Most High God (Genesis 14:18), although he is not of Aaron's lineage.
4. Sometimes the word designates a role of authority or responsibility: Shelemiah is called a "priest" when he oversees the temple storerooms (Nehemiah 13:13), as the head of a sacred administrative function.
H3548.origine: The Hebrew word כֹּהֵן (kohen) likely has a root meaning "to stand" or "to serve": the priest is one who stands before the living God to serve Him. From the Torah, the word primarily designates the sons of Aaron, ordained by Moses to offer sacrifices and maintain worship. The Septuagint (ancient Greek translation) renders this word as ἱερεύς (hiereus), which has given rise to the French words "hiérarchie" and "hiérarque". In the New Covenant, Jesus is presented as the Great Priest who fulfills this role definitively.
H3548.emploi: The word kohen appears 653 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Leviticus, Exodus, and the historical books. In the first five books (Pentateuch), it almost always designates the priests of Israel ordained by Moses or their descendants, notably the Aaronides. From the books of Kings and Chronicles, different lineages begin to emerge: the priests of Jerusalem, those of Jeroboam's temple in the north, and in later texts (Nehemiah), the leaders of worship after the exile. The word also applies, rarely but clearly, to foreign priests (Egyptians, Melchizedek) to show that other peoples recognized religious ministers.
H3548.portee: The priest reminds the believer that one does not approach God just any way: mediators, ordered worship, and purity rules are required. But it is also an image: in Jesus, the role of the priest changes entirely—there is no longer a need for a succession of priests, for Jesus offers once for all the sacrifice that reconciles definitively with God. The Christian thus understands that every believer has become a spiritual priest, capable of approaching God directly by faith.

sens: Man consecrated to God to make sacrifices and serve in the temple
Priest authorized to present offerings and burnt sacrifices at the altar
Man endowed with the authority and religious honor to perform divine worship
H3549.detail: 1. The priest is primarily a man chosen and set apart to perform sacrifices and burnt offerings in the temple, as an offering to God for the people. It is a delicate and solemn ministry: he must prepare young bulls, rams, and lambs, along with grain, salt, wine, and oil according to divine prescriptions (Ezra 6:9). 2. The priest also carries out the broader office of serving God in the temple, teaching the Law, and guiding public worship. In the book of Ezra, the priests are established according to their classes and divisions to ensure the service of the temple in Jerusalem (Ezra 6:18), alongside the Levites who assist them. 3. The term also denotes a status of honor and religious authority: Ezra himself, although primarily a scribe well-versed in the Law, receives the title of "priest" (Ezra 7:12), showing that this title carries respect and responsibility before God and the people.
H3549.origine: This Aramaic word is the form of the same language as the Hebrew word "kôhèn" (priest). It comes from an ancient root that evokes the idea of standing in a position of honor and service: the priest stands before God for the people, and before the people for God. The family of words includes the priesthood and the liturgical functions that discourage it.
H3549.emploi: The word appears eight times in Aramaic in the book of Ezra, part of the texts written in this language during the return from exile. It is found in the decrees of King Artaxerxes authorizing the return of the Israelites to Jerusalem and the restoration of temple worship. The priests are mentioned as beneficiaries of royal supplies (grain, oil, wine for sacrifices), as responsible for organizing religious service (classes and divisions), and as recipients of voluntary gifts from the people. Ezra himself is referred to as a priest, although his specialty is the knowledge of the written Law. The use of the term in Aramaic shows the continuity of the priestly ministry despite captivity and exile.
H3549.portee: This word reminds Christians that serving God requires consecrated and authorized individuals, set apart for this task. It also shows that the reconstruction of worship and the religious community after a trial begins with the establishment of order and proper service. For the evangelical reader, it prepares the understanding of the universal priesthood in Christ: Jesus is the great Priest who perfects and finalizes the service that the Old Testament expressed through these earthly figures.

sens: The charge, the office of priest, that is to say, of priest in the worship of Israel
The entirety of rights and duties attached to this office
The responsibility before God for transgressions committed in the service of the sanctuary
An everlasting covenant, a spiritual inheritance passed down to descendants
H3550.detail: 1. The priesthood is the charge entrusted to Aaron and his sons: it is the right and duty to serve in the sanctuary, to offer sacrifices, to approach God on behalf of the people. Exodus 29:9 states that "the priesthood shall be theirs by a perpetual statute" — it is an official function, recognized and inviolable. 2. This charge includes specific functions and serious responsibilities. Numbers 3:10 commands: "You shall appoint Aaron and his sons to observe their priesthood duties" — it is a defined work, with rites to be performed and an order to be respected. 3. The priesthood also carries a moral responsibility toward the Lord. Numbers 18:1 warns: "You shall bear the guilt of iniquity committed in the exercise of your priesthood" — the priests will answer before God if the worship is profaned or if they fail in their obligations. 4. For one who remains worthy, the priesthood becomes a lasting covenant passed down from age to age. Numbers 25:13 promises Phinehas: "It shall be to him and to his descendants after him a covenant of a perpetual priesthood" — it is a hereditary blessing, a bond with God that transcends generations.
H3550.origine: The Hebrew word כְּהֻנָּה (kehunna) comes from the root כהן (kohen), which means "priest" or "to serve as a priest." This root itself evokes the idea of standing and serving, of approaching to perform a sacred service. The same root appears in "כהן" (kohen), which designates the priest himself. The priesthood is therefore the service, the function that defines one who approaches the sanctuary to intercede on behalf of the people.
H3550.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the Pentateuch and historical books. It primarily designates the charge conferred to Aaron and his descendants (Exodus 29:9; Exodus 40:15) — an exclusive privilege that no one can usurp without risking death (Numbers 3:10). Numbers 16:10 reminds that God separated the Levites for the service of the sanctuary, thus distinguishing the priesthood from other functions. The usage evolves toward a broader sense: the priesthood becomes a moral responsibility (Numbers 18:1, 18:7), then a perpetual covenant for one who remains faithful (Numbers 25:13). After the exile, it is used to exclude from the community those whose priestly genealogy cannot be proven (Ezra 2:62; Nehemiah 7:64). The word always emphasizes the idea of a sacred charge, a dignity conferred by God, never taken by man.
H3550.portee: For the believer reading the Bible, the priesthood reminds that serving God requires both honor and responsibility. It is not a charge to be taken lightly: one who undertakes it answers before the Lord. For the Christian, these texts foreshadow the priesthood of Christ (Hebrews 5:5-6), the perfect priest who forever replaces the old Levitical order. Finally, they show that the people of God themselves are called to a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9), each tasked with interceding and serving faithfully.

sens: opening made in a wall to let in light and air
by extension, any bay or opening in a building
H3551.detail:
1. A window is an opening made in the wall of a house to allow daylight to enter and air to circulate. It is a building element as simple as it is useful: in Daniel 6:10, the windows of Daniel's upper chamber were open, allowing him to pray toward Jerusalem without leaving his house.
2. By extension, the word designates any bay or opening in a wall serving as a passage for light, even if it does not have as everyday a use as a regular window. It is the access through which light and air transform the interior of a dwelling.
H3551.origine: The Hebrew word is simple and concrete: it literally designates the opening of the window. In ancient Hebrew, as in the cultures of the Near East, the window was an important feature of houses, allowing rooms to be aired and enabling one to see outside without opening the door. The image is that of a bay through which light passes.
H3551.emploi: This word appears only once in the biblical Hebrew text, in Daniel 6:10, where it describes the windows of the upper chamber where Daniel prayed. Daniel, although he had received the order from King Darius not to pray, opened his windows toward Jerusalem and continued his three daily prayers. The open windows embody a simple truth: despite the obstacles, nothing could prevent Daniel from communicating with his God, not even a royal decree.
H3551.portee: This detail of the open windows reveals Daniel's trust and courage in the face of persecution. Rather than praying in secret, he maintains his orientation toward God and Jerusalem, knowing that his faithfulness could cost him his life. For the Christian, this image invites open and uncompromising prayer, regardless of context or danger.

sens: Region of North Africa mentioned in biblical prophecies
H3552.detail: Cush is a region or people of North Africa, likely located in Libya or nearby. It is mentioned in Ezekiel 30:5 among the military allies of Egypt, listed alongside Ethiopia, Put, and Lud, all of whom will fall together by the sword during God's judgment on Egypt.
H3552.origine: The Hebrew word כּוּשׁ (kush) is likely a variant or another spelling of לוּב (loub, "Libyan"). It designates a region or people of North Africa, probably related to ancient Libya.
H3552.emploi: Cush appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 30:5. The prophet lists it among nations and peoples that militarily supported Egypt and will together suffer its punishment. This prophetic context shows that Cush was known as a military ally of Egypt at the time of the prophet.

sens: Metal headgear that protects the head in battle
Symbolic protection granted by God to the warrior
Element of the complete armor of the soldier
H3553.detail:
1. The helmet is a military metal equipment — usually made of bronze — that covers and protects the head of the warrior in battle. Goliath wears "a bronze helmet" (1 Samuel 17:5), and Uzziah provides them for his soldiers (2 Chronicles 26:14). It is a concrete and heavy object, part of the warrior's arsenal along with the breastplate, shield, and spear.
2. In prophetic and symbolic language, the helmet becomes an image of divine protection. God puts on "the helmet of salvation" (Isaiah 59:17), meaning He takes on the role of a warrior to save His people and ensure their victory. The helmet then represents defense, covering, and assurance that God provides to those who trust Him.
3. The helmet is among the elements of the complete soldier's equipment, alongside the shield, breastplate, and offensive weapons. Ezekiel mentions shield and helmet together several times (Ezekiel 27:10; 38:5), showing that they form an inseparable set for the equipped warrior ready for battle.
H3553.origine: The Hebrew word כּוֹבַע (koba) literally means a rounded headgear. It likely comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or arching. The term is exclusively used for protective military equipment and is the standard term in biblical Hebrew for the warrior's helmet.
H3553.emploi: The word helmet appears 6 times in the Old Testament, always to refer to actual military equipment. It is used in war narratives (1 Samuel with Goliath, 2 Chronicles with Uzziah's troops, Jeremiah and Ezekiel in battle contexts), and in the prophetic passage of Isaiah where God Himself takes on the attributes of a warrior. The meaning remains concrete and physical in most cases, but Isaiah 59:17 elevates it to a spiritual and metaphorical sense, making it a symbol of God's saving protection.
H3553.portee: The helmet of salvation in Isaiah 59:17 speaks to every believer going through trial or spiritual battle: God does not ask His children to fight without protection. This image reminds us that trust in God, the certainty of His salvation and final victory, is like a helmet that protects the mind and heart. It is an invitation to put on the protection that God offers, rather than remain vulnerable to fear or doubt.

sens: To be consumed or damaged by fire or intense heat
To be marked or severely affected by an injury or pain
H3554.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the physical action of fire that consumes or damages: when someone walks on hot coals, their feet are "burned" (Proverbs 6:28). It is the sensation and concrete effect of extreme heat on the body.
2. By extension, it designates any serious or deep injury, physical or moral: in Isaiah 43:2, the Lord promises that if His people walk through the fire, they will not be "burned," meaning they will not suffer the damage or destruction that fire would normally bring. The image of fire here represents trials and threats, and not being burned means being protected from them.
H3554.origine: The Hebrew verb comes from a root that evokes the action of fire on materials: to burn, consume, mark. The form we encounter is in the Niphal, a passive voice in Hebrew, which means that the subject undergoes the action ("to be burned") rather than causing it. This voice emphasizes vulnerability and lack of defense against the threat of fire.
H3554.emploi: The verb appears twice in the provided biblical texts, both in the passive voice ("to be burned"). In Proverbs 6:28, it describes a concrete and physical situation: one who walks on hot coals will have their feet burned — it is a natural and inevitable fact. In Isaiah 43:2, the same word is used to speak of divine protection: God promises that His servant will not be burned by fire, transforming the physical image into a spiritual promise. In both cases, the word emphasizes a threatening reality (destructive heat) and the question of who will escape it or not.
H3554.portee: This word teaches that the fire of judgment and trial is a fearful reality, but that God can spare His children from destruction. In Isaiah, the promise "you will not be burned" becomes a symbol of divine protection in life's crises: it assures the believer that God's power is stronger than any threat. It is an invitation to trust rather than fear.

sens: mark or lesion caused by fire or intense heat
scar or trace left by a burn
injury inflicted intentionally by fire
H3555.detail: 1. A burn is primarily the physical lesion produced by fire or intense heat on the body. It is the injury itself, fresh and painful. 2. The word also designates the scar or mark that persists after a burn has healed: the visible and permanent trace of fire on the skin. In Exodus 21:25, the burn is part of the bodily injuries that must be compensated according to the law of retaliation ("burn for burn"), which shows that it is considered a serious and recognizable injury. 3. The term can finally refer to a voluntary burn, an act of violence by fire, since biblical law mentions it as a punishable harm.
H3555.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to burn" or "to be burned." It is formed to precisely describe the visible result of fire on the body: the mark and the scar. The same root produces the verb that means to be inflamed or to burn, and the noun always refers to the bodily effect of fire on human flesh.
H3555.emploi: The word appears once in the Bible, in Exodus 21:25, at the heart of the law of retaliation concerning serious injuries. It enumerates the compensations that a victim must receive: "eye for eye, tooth for tooth, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise." The burn is listed alongside serious mutilations of the face and limbs, showing that it was considered a serious injury justifying equivalent compensation or punishment.
H3555.portee: This word reminds us that the Law of Moses took bodily harm seriously and demanded equitable justice. The burn, a permanent and visible scar, symbolizes the deep wounds we carry: it speaks to the Christian of the need for restitution and healing, and shows that the God of Israel did not leave violence unpunished.

sens: luminous celestial body that shines at night
celestial body representing a person or a destiny
innumerable multitude
excellence, luminous splendor
H3556.detail:
1. The star is primarily a celestial body, a heavenly creation that God made to illuminate the night (Genesis 1:16). It shines in the sky and remains pure in the eyes of God, unlike larger celestial bodies (Job 25:5).
2. The star can symbolically represent a person or embody a destiny: Joseph's dream shows stars bowing down (Genesis 37:9), and Balaam prophesies that a star will rise out of Jacob, announcing the Messiah (Numbers 24:17).
3. The star expresses the idea of an innumerable multitude: God promises Abraham a descendants as numerous as the stars in the sky, an image of an unimaginable quantity (Genesis 15:5; 1 Chronicles 27:23).
4. The star symbolizes glory and excellence: in Daniel's vision, those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars (Daniel 12:3), signifying eternal splendor.
H3556.origine: The Hebrew word kokháv comes from a root that evokes something that sparkles or shines. Its etymology emphasizes the luminous nature of the star. In the Old Testament, the star is always a divine creation, never a deity itself as in neighboring religions: it reveals the wisdom and power of the Creator God who "counts the number of the stars" and calls each by name (Psalms 147:4).
H3556.emploi: The word kokháv appears 37 times in the Old Testament, primarily in Genesis, the Psalms, and the prophets. It first designates stars as created celestial realities (Genesis 1:16; Deuteronomy 4:19). Then, the meaning enriches: the stars become a measure of the impossible and the infinite, in the promises of descendants (Genesis 15:5; Exodus 32:13). Balaam's prophecy (Numbers 24:17) transforms the star into a messianic figure, opening a powerful symbolic usage. Finally, the prophets use the extinction of stars as a sign of cosmic and divine upheaval (Isaiah 13:10; Joel 2:10).
H3556.portee: For the Christian, the star reminds of the greatness of divine creation and the infinity of God's providence. It invites reflection on God's promises made to Abraham: a descendants as numerous as the stars, an image of the Church in Christ. The prophecy of the star rising out of Jacob, echoed in the birth of the Messiah (Matthew 2), shows that celestial signs serve the divine plan of salvation. Finally, the promise that the righteous will shine like the stars encourages the believer to seek God's glory and eternity.

sens: To hold enclosed, to retain within the limits of something
To support, nourish, provide for someone's maintenance
To carry, bear, endure something difficult
To be capable of receiving or supporting in quantity
H3557.detail:
1. To retain or enclose something inside: this is the idea of setting a limit, of keeping something inside. Jeremiah says that the word of God in his heart is "shut up in his bones" and that he "strives to contain it," meaning to hold it back (Jeremiah 20:9); David "provided for the maintenance" of his concubines by keeping them enclosed (2 Samuel 20:3).
2. To support someone by providing the necessities for living: food, shelter, what allows one to subsist. Joseph tells his brothers: "I will nourish you" during the famine (Genesis 45:11); the Lord "nourishes" the people for forty years in the desert (Nehemiah 9:21).
3. To bear, endure a difficult or painful reality: the heart of man "endures" depression (Proverbs 18:14), and Jeremiah "strives to contain" the burning word within him.
4. To have the physical capacity to receive or hold inside: the bronze altar was "too small to contain" the sacrifices (1 Kings 8:64); the heavens cannot "contain" God as great as He is (2 Chronicles 2:6).
H3557.origine: The Hebrew verb kul comes from a root that evokes the idea of holding, mastering, keeping in one's hands or arms. It carries the image of someone who retains something or someone to keep it under control. The family of the word includes intensive and causative forms that enrich the meaning: to fully contain, to maintain durably, or to make hold together. It is a concrete word, rooted in the physical experience of the body that holds, carries, and nourishes.
H3557.emploi: The verb kul appears 37 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in historical narratives and wisdom literature. It first designates the action of nourishing and maintaining someone: Joseph nourishes his brothers and father during the famine (Genesis 45:11, 47:12), the king nourishes his servants (1 Kings 4:27), Elijah is nourished by ravens (1 Kings 17:4). It then expresses the physical capacity to contain or hold: a basin of bronze contains so many measures (1 Kings 7:26), the altar is too small to contain the sacrifices (1 Kings 8:64). The word is also used figuratively to express what one endures or retains internally: the psalmist "holds back" the psalm of God on his lips (Psalms 55:23), Jeremiah "contains" the burning divine word within him (Jeremiah 20:9). The common image is that of something that holds, persists, supports.
H3557.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that God, like a father, supports and nourishes those who depend on Him — not only with material food but also with moral and spiritual strength. The idea that our heart "can endure" speaks to the capacity that God gives us in the face of trials. Conversely, the word of God is so alive that it cannot really be "contained" for long: it demands to be expressed. This word thus speaks of dependence, providence, and the irrepressible power of the word of God.

sens: Gold ornament worn on the wrist or arm
Gold object given as a gift or for consecration
Valuable item included in an offering to God
H3558.detail:
1. The bracelet is a gold ornament worn around the wrist or arm, like rings and earrings mentioned in the same passages (Exodus 35:22; Numbers 31:50). It is a precious object, a symbol of wealth and elegance.

2. In the two biblical uses, the bracelet always appears in a list of precious gold objects — along with rings, chains, earrings — offered as a gift to God. In Exodus 35:22, the people bring bracelets for the construction of the tabernacle; in Numbers 31:50, the army leaders offer them for atonement.

3. The bracelet thus represents a material possession of great value that the believer voluntarily dedicates to the Lord. This gesture shows the commitment of the heart: one relinquishes what belongs to them, what adorns and beautifies them, to honor God.
H3558.origine: The Hebrew word kûmâz (כּוּמָז) has an uncertain etymology; its exact form and primary meaning are not clearly documented in other ancient texts. It is assumed to refer to an object worn on the arms or wrists, but the word appears rarely in the Old Testament and has no obvious root. This is why the Segond sometimes translates it as "bracelet" and sometimes as "necklace," both being precious ornaments offered to God.
H3558.emploi: The word kûmâz appears only twice in the Bible (Exodus 35:22 and Numbers 31:50), always in a context of voluntary offering. In Exodus 35:22, during the construction of the tabernacle, the Israelites — men and women, with willing hearts — bring bracelets among other precious gold objects. In Numbers 31:50, after the victory over Midian, the military leaders offer gold bracelets to the Lord for the atonement of the army's sins. In both cases, the bracelet appears in a list of valuable ornaments, never alone, and symbolizes the wealth that is made available to God.
H3558.portee: The bracelet reminds the reader that consecration to God also touches our material wealth and precious possessions. It is not a legal obligation, but a heartfelt offering: those whose hearts were willing (Exodus 35:22) gave freely. Offering one's bracelet is to acknowledge that everything comes from God and that nothing is too precious for Him.

sens: To set up, organize the necessary elements for something
To make something stable, solid, established in a lasting way
To be ready, to be prepared to act
To direct towards a goal, to orient correctly
To arrange, to dispose in order
H3559A.detail:
1. To prepare means to gather and organize what is necessary before an important moment. Joseph tells his steward: "prepare" the meal to receive his brothers (Genesis 43:16); each week, the Levites "prepare" the showbread (1 Chronicles 9:32). It is a concrete and practical task.

2. The word also means to make something stable and lasting, as one establishes a foundation. The ant "prepares" its food in the summer so that it is there in the winter (Proverbs 6:8): it creates a solid reserve.

3. To be prepared or ready means to be in a state of being able to act or serve without delay. Job speaks of "preparing a seat for himself," settling into a position of power and stability (Job 29:7).

4. The word can also mean to direct something towards an end, to orient it correctly. It is to guide or regulate, in a moral sense, what is to happen.

5. To arrange and order things according to a plan is also to prepare: to set one's affairs, approach, or path in order before moving forward.
H3559A.origine: The Hebrew word kun comes from a root that evokes the idea of founding, of setting firmly in place. It appears in several forms: the simple form (Qal) expresses the meaning of "becoming stable" or "being established," while the derived forms (Hiphil, Niphal, etc.) show a more voluntary action or a more marked passivity. The verb fundamentally describes the action of making something reliable, unchanging, trustworthy — like a foundation upon which one can rely.
H3559A.emploi: The verb kun appears 82 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is mostly found in the historical books (Chronicles, Kings, Nehemiah), the Psalms, Proverbs, and the prophets. In Chronicles, it describes the preparation of the elements of the temple: the wood, the gold, the instruments, the bread offered to God. In Proverbs, it depicts wisdom and foresight: the ant that prepares, the heart that prepares to seek God. In the Psalms, it can mean "to set in order" one's bow or traps in the sense of judgment. The word oscillates between concrete and material action (preparing a meal, arranging materials) and figurative meaning (establishing a righteous heart, strengthening a moral intention).
H3559A.portee: This word speaks to the Christian of a forgotten biblical reality: preparing is not anxiety; it is a form of faith. Like the ant that prepares without worrying, the believer can put their life, service, and heart in order, in trust. God himself "prepares" and "establishes" what lasts. It is a call to peaceful responsibility and wisdom: there is a time to prepare, and this preparation does not contradict trust in God.

sens: One who has success, prosperity, everything goes wonderfully
One who enjoys a stable and trouble-free life
H3559B.detail:
1. The word in Hebrew designates one who lives in ease and security, whom everything seems to favor. In Job 12:5, the expression "the saying of the happy" speaks of those whom life spares, who have not known misfortune: it is the tranquil and fulfilled man, whose affairs prosper.
2. More broadly, it is one whose life flows without great shocks or upheavals — a state of stability and relative peace that only one who possesses resources and health can truly savor.
H3559B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that initially evokes the idea of firmness, solidity, of what holds strong — the image of a stable foundation. From there arises the meaning of "well established," "at ease." It is found in other Hebrew forms meaning "fixed," "stable"; the noun thus describes one whose life, like a foundation, is well set.
H3559B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 12:5. In this passage, Job ironically comments on the human condition by noting that the happy — those whom misfortune has never touched — easily scorn the unfortunate and speak of those who stumble with disdain. The usage thus highlights the contrast between the security of the well-off and the fragility of those whom fate has struck.
H3559B.portee: This word reminds us that material prosperity and stability should never make us insensitive to the suffering of others. Job denounces here the indifference of the "happy": the Christian is called to empathize with the unfortunate instead of despising them, and to recognize that true blessedness is not in earthly wealth, but in justice and faithfulness to God.

sens: To become firm, stable, solid
To stand firm, to hold on, to endure
To be prepared, ready, arranged
To establish, to set in place, to found
To direct, orient, apply towards a goal
To obtain certainty, to rely on something
H3559H.detail:
1. To become firm, stable, solid: this is the idea that something moves from a fragile or unstable state to a robust and lasting state. In 1 Kings 2:24, Solomon says that the Lord has "strengthened" him on the throne: the throne no longer wobbles, it is secure under his feet.
2. To stand firm, to hold on, to endure: what is established persists and does not collapse. Psalm 93:1 says this of the world: "The world is established; it will not wobble."
3. To be prepared, ready, arranged: when something is strengthened, it is also put in order, ready to function. In Exodus 15:17, God establishes the sanctuary, that is, prepares and sets it up to serve.
4. To establish, to set in place, to found: active sense, the one who acts strengthens something or someone. The Lord establishes a throne that lasts (2 Samuel 7:12-13).
5. To direct, orient, apply towards a goal: moral and spiritual sense: to strengthen one's heart towards God (2 Chronicles 19:3), is to turn it, to fix it firmly in its direction.
6. To obtain certainty, to rely on something: to be sure that something will happen or that one can trust it. This is particularly clear in God's promises.
H3559H.origine: The root kun expresses the idea of "standing up" and "remaining stable." It gathers images of solidity: a foundation that does not move, a line that does not deviate, a heart that does not waver. In Hebrew, the verb unfolds in several forms: simple form (Niphal) to say that something becomes stable, causative form (Hiphil) to say that someone establishes something, and other intensive or reflexive forms (Polel, Hithpolel) that enrich the picture. The word appears 97 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms and in royal narratives, as it expresses the solidity of thrones and divine promises.
H3559H.emploi: The verb appears 97 times, mostly in the Psalms (where it speaks of the stability of God and his decrees), in royal history (where it establishes the thrones of David and his sons), and in Proverbs (where it establishes houses and plans). Concrete sense: to establish a house (Proverbs 24:3), to found a sanctuary (Exodus 15:17). Political sense: to strengthen a king on his throne (1 Kings 2:24, 2 Samuel 7:12-13). Spiritual sense: to strengthen one's heart towards God (2 Chronicles 19:3, Psalms 108:2), or to turn it in the command of God (Proverbs 4:26). Cosmic sense: God has strengthened the world, the earth, the heavens (Psalms 93:1-2, Proverbs 3:19). The word oscillates between the passive idea of becoming stable and the active idea of firmly establishing something.
H3559H.portee: This word brings the believer a precious assurance: the promises and thrones that God establishes are not fragile or temporary; they are strengthened to last. It also invites one to turn their own heart towards God firmly, not through instability or hesitation. In the prayer of the Psalms, "to strengthen" one's heart becomes a request: give me certainty, solidity in faith and in justice.

sens: Establish something solidly, giving it a stable and lasting foundation
Prepare, arrange, organize for something to be ready to function
Create, form, produce something new
Strengthen, fortify, make more robust or assured
Direct towards a goal, orient firmly (in a moral sense)
H3559I.detail:
1. Establishing solidly: this means laying the foundations of a city or institution so that it stands firm. When Sihon rebuilt his city (Numbers 21:27), he fortified it to make it a stable place. It is the image of a construction that takes root.

2. Preparing and arranging: this means putting in order what needs to function. When the temple service is restored (2 Chronicles 29:35), everything is reorganized so that worship can resume regularly.

3. Creating and forming: this means producing something from nothing or raw material. God creates the heavens and the stars (Psalms 8:4), he creates man (Psalms 119:73). It is the creative act that gives existence and form.

4. Strengthening and fortifying: this means making something stronger, more robust. God strengthens the exhausted heritage of his people (Psalms 68:10) to restore vigor and stability to them.

5. Firmly orienting: this means directing something or someone towards a determined goal, with the idea of moral firmness or unwavering resolution.
H3559I.origine: The Hebrew verb koun comes from a root that evokes the idea of standing up, being upright, taking a position. The family of the word includes forms that express stability, solidity, and preparation. The basic image is that of something that stands up, asserts itself, becomes firm and durable — from which the meaning of establishing, founding, preparing something to endure derives.
H3559I.emploi: This verb appears 14 times in the cited usages. It is used mainly in the Psalms and the prophets to speak of God's creative action: he founds the world by his wisdom (Jeremiah 10:12), creates the heavens (Psalms 8:4), creates man (Psalms 119:73). It also applies to the establishment of human institutions: the reconstruction of a city (Numbers 21:27), the restoration of the temple service (2 Chronicles 29:35). The word oscillates between the concrete idea of building, founding, or preparing, and the broader idea of creating or forming. In all these cases, it implies an intention of solidity and durability.
H3559I.portee: This word reminds the reader that all order, all stability, all creation comes from God's action. When we read that God "founds" the world or "creates" man, we understand that there is no chance, but an intention, a wisdom that organizes and builds. For the Christian, this means that his own existence, like that of the cosmos, rests on God's founding act. It is a source of confidence and humility.

sens: Make stable and solid, without fluctuation
