2. Figuratively, a spark can symbolize a visible manifestation of a hidden or immense power. A small spark betrays the existence of a great fire; it is like the external sign of it. In the context of Leviathan, these sparks reveal the superhuman and almost divine strength of this creature.
H3590.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root expressing the idea of jumping or escaping. A spark is by nature what flies away, what comes from the mother fire and scatters. It is the image of a small thing that flees, that suddenly appears — an instantaneous and fleeting manifestation of the energy of fire.
H3590.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 41:10. It describes the sparks of fire that escape from the mouth of Leviathan. It is a hapax — a unique word — that serves to reinforce the impression of raw power and sacred terror that Leviathan inspires. The poetic context of the Book of Job, where God addresses Job about his own smallness in the face of the wonders of creation, makes this word even more striking: the sparks of the monster symbolize a reality far beyond human understanding.
H3590.portee: This word reminds the reader that even the smallest visible manifestations can testify to immense and hidden power. When Job contemplates the sparks of Leviathan, he measures the staggering gap between himself and the creative wisdom of God. For today's believer, the sparks invite us to see in the small signs of creation hints of the greatness of the Creator.

sens: throwing weapon: short spear or pointed dart thrown by hand
stick or pointed rod that one wields or holds
rigid piece of armor that protects the neck and throat
H3591.detail:
1. The javelin is a throwing weapon, a kind of short and pointed spear that a soldier holds in hand and throws at the enemy. In the account of the conquest of Ai, Joshua raises a javelin toward the city (Joshua 8:18), and he holds it out toward heaven until the end of the battle, as a signal calling for divine victory (Joshua 8:26). It is an ordinary weapon of war, which the Philistines carried along with the sword and spear (1 Samuel 17:45).
2. The word also refers to a dart or a pointed spear, that is, a shorter and lighter pointed rod that is thrown or launched. Job 41:20 speaks of the darts that the crocodile does not fear, thus showing its invincible strength.
3. In 1 Samuel 17:6, the word refers to a piece of armor that protects the neck and throat, a kind of rigid bronze throat guard. This is a different use of the same Hebrew word, showing how a pointed object can also serve to defend the body.
H3591.origine: The Hebrew word מִדְיוֹן (kidon) probably comes from a root that evokes the action of pointing or striking. Its basic image is that of a point or a rod that pierces. The same root has given rise to other words related to pointed or sharp objects. The word transitions from the throwing weapon to the figurative sense of what pricks or wounds.
H3591.emploi: The word appears about 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in accounts of war and hunting. It appears in the Greek Old Testament translating the same Hebrew word. The historical books (Joshua, 1 Samuel) present it as an ordinary weapon of the soldier or fighter, which Joshua raises as a sign of victory. The book of Job uses it to evoke the weapons of powerful warriors (Job 39:26) or to show the strength of formidable animals (Job 41:20). In some cases, like that of Goliath, it is part of armor equipment, not a throwing weapon.
H3591.portee: The javelin, whether a weapon or armor, reminds the reader that victory in the spiritual battles of faith comes not from military strength but from obedience to God. Joshua holding his javelin raised toward heaven shows that this gesture is only useful because the Lord acts. This image invites the Christian to place their true weapon — the Word and trust in God — above any human strength.

sens: Place where the incident of transporting the ark of the covenant took place
Area or land belonging to someone
H3592.detail:
1. Kidon is the place where, during the transport of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, the Levite Uzzah reached out to steady it when the oxen stumbled — an act that cost him his life (1 Chronicles 13:9). It has become a famous location in the history of Israel due to this dramatic event.
2. The word also refers to an area or piece of land, probably the land of a person named Nacon (also called Kidon) — a landowner where grain was threshed or where significant agricultural or cultic activities took place.
H3592.origine: The Hebrew word כִּידֹן (kidon) would originally mean "spear" or "javelin" according to some scholars, but in biblical texts, it primarily designates a specific place. It is the name of an area or land. In 2 Samuel 6:6, the same event is referred to as "the threshing floor of Nacon" (נָכוֹן - Nacon), and 1 Chronicles 13:9 mentions "the threshing floor of Kidon" for the same incident, suggesting that Kidon and Nacon refer to the same location, likely named after a person who owned it.
H3592.emploi: Kidon appears only once in the Segond (1 Chronicles 13:9), in the account of the transport of the ark of the covenant. This event is also recounted in 2 Samuel 6:6, where the place is called "the threshing floor of Nacon." Both texts describe the same crucial moment: Uzzah, seeing the ark tipping on the cart pulled by the oxen, reaches out to steady it, which leads to his immediate death, as only consecrated priests could touch the ark. This place becomes a memorial marker of God's absolute holiness and the respect He demands.
H3592.portee: The incident at Kidon teaches the Christian reader about the fearsome holiness of God and the importance of obeying His precise instructions in worship and divine service. Although Uzzah acted with good intentions, his unauthorized gesture results in immediate divine judgment — a reminder that the sincerity of the heart does not replace obedience to the Word and the role assigned by God. It is a passage that confronts the reader with the gravity of sin and the majesty of a God who does not tolerate the transgression of His ordinances.

sens: sudden and violent attack
combat charge
overwhelming affliction
H3593.detail:
1. The assault is a sudden and violent attack, often launched by an army or a strong enemy. In Job 15:24, distress and anguish "assail like a king ready for battle": they descend upon the unfortunate man like an irresistible military charge.
2. The word also evokes the battle charge itself, the moment when soldiers rush at the enemy with all their might. It is the raw image of combat violence.
3. Figuratively, anything that strikes someone with force — misfortunes, sorrow, panic — can be described as an assault that overwhelms and knocks them down.
H3593.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of a violent charge, a sudden attack. It belongs to the family of words that depict combat and aggression. It is a classic military term in biblical Hebrew, conveying the visceral image of warriors rushing to strike.
H3593.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Job 15:24. Eliphaz, Job's friend, describes the terrors that assail the wicked: distress and anguish attack him "like a king ready for battle." Here, the military assault becomes a powerful figure to show how misfortunes descend upon one who has turned away from God, with the same violence as a military invasion.
H3593.portee: This word teaches that tribulations can strike us with overwhelming force. But the attentive reader will note that in the context of the book of Job, this description of the assaults of misfortune on the wicked is voiced by a friend who judges too quickly: it invites us not to confuse the violence of misfortune with a certain judgment from God.

sens: Babylonian idol representing Saturn
H3594.detail: 1. Kiyyoun is the name of a foreign deity, probably a representation of the Babylonian god of the planet Saturn. It is a statue or image that unfaithful Israelites carried during their religious pilgrimages, as reported by the prophet Amos.
H3594.origine: The Hebrew word כִּיּוּן (kiyyoun) designates an idol or a stone pillar. This term comes from the Assyro-Babylonian religious context: it refers to a foreign deity whose worship had infiltrated among the Israelites. The word reflects how neighboring peoples conceived and represented their gods in material and visual forms.
H3594.emploi: Kiyyoun appears only once in the Bible, in Amos 5:26, where the prophet denounces the Israelites who carry this idol with them during their religious processions. Amos mentions it among other practices of idolatry: the Israelites worshiped foreign gods and made carved images. This unique reference shows how the prophetic text uses the specific name of a false deity to characterize the spiritual unfaithfulness of the chosen people.
H3594.portee: Kiyyoun symbolizes the abandonment of the true God for foreign powers. The fact that the Israelites physically carried this idol shows how visible and organized religious apostasy can become. For the Christian, this word reminds us that idolatry is never accidental: it involves a conscious choice to turn away from God to follow false powers.

sens: Bronze vessel used to hold water or other liquids
Large basin or reservoir on a pedestal
Fire pit or hearth containing fire or coals
Raised platform or stage
H3595.detail:
1. In the tabernacle and the temple, the basin (or laver) of bronze is the large vessel where the priests wash before approaching the altar or serving in worship. In Exodus 30:18, Moses is commanded to place this basin "between the tent of meeting and the altar" filled with water; it is a holy object, anointed with holy oil like the altar itself (Leviticus 8:11).
2. In the time of Solomon, several large basins were made: 1 Kings 7:38 describes "ten bronze basins" of forty baths each (one bath ≈ 37 liters), set on ornate bronze bases, testifying to the wealth and organization of the royal temple.
3. It was also used as a hearth or fire pit containing coals, serving to burn incense or offerings: this is the usage of the word in Zechariah 12:6, which refers to fire pits.
4. Rarely, it designates a raised platform or stage, as in 2 Chronicles 6:13 where it serves as a podium.
H3595.origine: The Hebrew word כִּיֹּר (kiyyor) likely comes from a root expressing the idea of digging or forming a hollow vessel. The word is specific to Israelite worship and the temple installations; it appears mainly in the historical and legislative books describing the service of the sanctuary. Its root evokes the practical action of containing or holding a liquid.
H3595.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in Exodus (for the laver of the tabernacle), 1 Kings, and 2 Chronicles (for the basins of the temple in Jerusalem). In the time of Moses, it designates the unique and holy basin for the priests' ablution; under Solomon, ten were made, installed in the renovated temple. The word is also used for fire pits or vessels of fire (Zechariah), and rarely for a platform (2 Chronicles 6:13). Its usage remains concentrated in passages describing organized worship and sacred equipment.
H3595.portee: The basin reminds the reader that pure worship requires prior purification: before approaching God, one must wash. In the spiritual life of the Christian, this detail evokes the constant need to purify oneself through the Word of God (as the Church "without spot or wrinkle... holy and blameless," Ephesians 5:27). This basin, an object of daily service yet consecrated, also teaches that God cares about the practical details of worship and concrete holiness.

sens: Dishonest and deceptive person
One who acts with calculated malice
Individual whose weapons are deception and lies
H3596.detail:
1. A deceitful person is someone dishonest, who hides their evil intentions under deceptive appearances. In Isaiah 32:5, the text refuses to give the deceitful a title of nobility: they do not deserve to be honored as a good person, for they are not one.
2. The deceitful acts with calculated malice: they do not deceive by chance, but by intention, forming harmful plans. Isaiah 32:7 shows that "the weapons of the deceitful are pernicious" — they use deception as a weapon to do harm.
3. The deceitful particularly prey on the weak, perverting justice: they "cause the unfortunate to perish with false words," even when their cause is just (Isaiah 32:7). They are predators who exploit their ability to deceive to crush those who cannot defend themselves.
H3596.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of emptiness, hollowness, absence of substance — and thus of falsehood: someone who is empty of sincerity, whose words are hollow. This image of emptiness well reveals the nature of the deceitful: they may shine with their words, but there is nothing solid in them, no truth.
H3596.emploi: This word appears only twice in Isaiah 32, in the depiction of the false honors of the wicked world. The prophetic text clearly distinguishes the noble from the deceitful, the good man from the deceiver: it is a moral condemnation, a warning against those who enjoy a usurped reputation. The prophet denounces those who bear titles they do not deserve, who seduce with words while exercising malice.
H3596.portee: This word reminds the reader that true nobility of character is not a matter of title, reputation, or appearance, but of sincerity and justice. It warns against manipulators who exploit words and appearances to dominate the weak. It is an exhortation to discern the true from the false, and to resist the influence of those whose only merit is deception.

sens: Large tool made of wood and metal used for chopping, splitting, or crushing
Instrument of destruction or violence
H3597.detail:
1. The axe is a thick metal blade fixed to the end of a wooden handle, used for chopping down trees, splitting wood, or striking. It is a tool of the farmer and the lumberjack, but also a fearsome weapon. In Psalm 74:6, the enemies destroy the temple with axes, the same tools that were used to conquer the promised land.
2. Figuratively, the axe symbolizes ruthless destruction and violence. In this psalm, it represents the work of enemies who ravage God's sanctuary with brutality, showing no respect for its holiness.
H3597.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to strike" or "to cut." It literally designates the tool of the lumberjack, the instrument that slices and divides wood. The axe was well known in Israel as a working tool and, unfortunately, as a weapon of war.
H3597.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 74:6, to describe the damage done by enemies in the temple. This psalm is a cry of distress: the sanctuary has been profaned, and the enemies have struck it with axes as one demolishes a building. The image is one of brute violence, of the systematic destruction of a holy place.
H3597.portee: The psalmist reminds us that God's enemies dare to attack his sanctuary with violence. This image helps the reader to grasp the gravity of the sacrilege and the dismay of the people in the face of the profanation. It also invites us to recognize that even if enemies destroy places of worship, God himself cannot be destroyed: his word remains.

sens: group of seven stars visible in the night sky
celestial constellation serving as a guide for navigators and farmers
H3598.detail:
1. The Pleiades form a cluster of stars visible to the naked eye in the night sky, particularly recognizable for their proximity. Job 9:9 mentions them alongside Ursa Major and Orion among the great constellations created by God.
2. As an identifiable constellation, the Pleiades served as a landmark for the ancients for navigation and marking agricultural seasons. Their appearance and disappearance in the sky signaled key moments of the year. Job 38:31 speaks of them poetically: one cannot bind or loose their ties as one would with a sail, emphasizing their distant and majestic nature, beyond human reach.
H3598.origine: The Hebrew word Kimah specifically designates this stellar cluster. Its etymology refers to the idea of a group or a tightly-knit assembly. The Greek name Pleiades (from Greek pleios, "many") literally means "the numerous ones." In several ancient cultures, notably in Egypt and Mesopotamia, these seven stars held great religious and practical significance.
H3598.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in wisdom or prophetic books (Job and Amos). In each occurrence, the Pleiades serve to illustrate God's greatness and creative power. In Job 9:9 and Amos 5:8, the same context is found: God created these stars and governs them. In Job 38:31, God poses a question to Job to bring him back to humility in the face of the immensity of his creation. The word always evokes the immutable celestial order and divine mastery over the cosmos.
H3598.portee: The Pleiades remind the believer that only God orders the visible and invisible universe, and that human science and technology cannot rival his creative work. This word invites awe-filled contemplation of creation and humility in the face of the mysteries of God that infinitely surpass us.

sens: Small portable bag for holding money or precious items
Container for weights used to measure and weigh goods
H3599.detail:
1. The word designates a small bag that one carries to store money or valuable items. In Isaiah 46:6, the idolaters pour the gold from their pouch to give it to a goldsmith: it is the bag where they kept their riches.
2. It can also describe the container that holds the weights used in commerce. In Deuteronomy 25:13 and Micah 6:11, the Law condemns having "false weights in the pouch": the dishonest merchant carries his rigged weights in a pouch to cheat on the weight of the goods sold. It is a breach of trust.
H3599.origine: The Hebrew word kis comes from a root that evokes the idea of containing or enclosing. Its image is that of a small closed bag, portable, distinctly different from a large jug or chest. It is an everyday object in the ancient Near Eastern world.
H3599.emploi: The word appears five times in the Old Testament, mainly to denounce commercial dishonesty. Deuteronomy 25:13, Proverbs 16:11, and Micah 6:11 use it in the context of weights and measures, warning against false balances and rigged weights carried in one's pouch — a known practice of fraud. Isaiah 46:6 uses it for the money invested in the making of idols. Proverbs 1:14 refers to a common pouch, symbolizing association or sharing of plunder. The context always reveals a moral question: righteousness or dishonesty.
H3599.portee: This pouch is never neutral in the eyes of biblical Law. It calls the believer to commercial honesty and the refusal of dishonest enrichment — even when fraud would be easy and profitable. It also reminds us that money and wealth engage our moral responsibility before God.

sens: son of David and Eglah
one of the six eldest sons of David born in Hebron
H3507.detail: 1. Jithream is one of the sons of King David, born to his wife Eglah while he reigned in Hebron, before the conquest of Jerusalem. He appears in the list of David's children as the sixth son according to 2 Samuel 3:5, or the fifth according to 1 Chronicles 3:3 — a variation that reflects different ways of counting these children in ancient traditions.
H3507.origine: The name Jithream means "profit of the people" or "excellence of the people" in Hebrew, combining the idea of profit or superiority with that of the people. This name, like many royal Israelite names, expressed a blessing or an aspiration for the child at birth.
H3507.emploi: Jithream is mentioned twice in Scripture: in 2 Samuel 3:5 and in 1 Chronicles 3:3, both in genealogical lists of David's sons. These lists enumerate the children born to David in Hebron, before his establishment in Jerusalem. Unlike his brothers Amnon, Absalom, Adonijah, and Solomon, who play significant roles in the biblical narrative, Jithream is mentioned only by name and birth order. He represents one of the many descendants of King David, most of whom remain in the background of history.

sens: man of the tribe of Asher during the time of the divided monarchy
son of Zophah and brother of many other sons of the same father
father of Jephunné, Pispa, and Ara
H3506H.detail:
1. Jithran is a man of the tribe of Asher mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Asher during the time of the divided monarchy (1 Chronicles 7:37). He appears in a list of Asherite families, indicating his importance in the history of this tribe.
2. He is the son of Zophah and is part of a large sibling group; the Bible lists his brothers: Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilsha, and Beera. This enumeration highlights the fertility and expansion of the Asherite family.
3. Jithran is also the father of three sons: Jephunné, Pispa, and Ara, which shows his lineage and his place in the genealogical chain of Asher.
H3506H.origine: The name Jithran means "advantage" in Hebrew. He is sometimes referred to as Jether (יֶתֶר) in other genealogical passages. The name likely reflects the parents' hope for a blessing or advantage for their son.
H3506H.emploi: Jithran is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:37, in the midst of a genealogy of the sons of Asher. This mention is part of a lengthy genealogical passage (1 Chronicles 7) that lists the main families of Israel after the return from exile. His appearance in this official list indicates that he was an important figure in the tribe of Asher, likely a recognized family leader or patriarch. Although nothing is known of his personal deeds, his presence in the genealogy connects him to the history of the people of Israel.
H3506H.portee: The mention of Jithran reminds us that the Bible is concerned with the continuity of the tribes and families of Israel, even after the exile. It invites the reader to see how God has preserved the genealogical lines of His people and how each family, even those less known, fits into the grand design of Israel's restoration.

sens: Descendants of Jether, ancestor of the clan
Member of the clan of Jether
Inhabitant of, or native to, the territory of the clan of Jether
H3505.detail:
1. The Ithrites are the descendants of an ancestor named Jether. The term designates a whole family line going back to this founding ancestor. In 1 Chronicles 2:53 they are listed among the families of Kiriath-jearim, in the same way as the Puthites and the Shumathites.
2. The word also designates an individual member of this clan. Ira and Gareb, two of David's elite warriors (2 Samuel 23:38), are both presented as "the Ithrite", that is, belonging to the clan of the Ithrites. It is a way of indicating their family origin and their attachment to this group.
H3505.origine: The word Ithrites comes from the name Jether, which may mean "abundance" or "excellence" in Hebrew. It is a common genealogical term in Israel: the name of a clan is formed by adding a suffix to the name of its founding ancestor, as with "Benjamites" (descendants of Benjamin) or "Judeans" (descendants of Judah). This practice reflects the way the Israelites organized their society around families and clans.
H3505.emploi: The term appears three times in the Old Testament. Twice it designates individuals: Ira and Gareb, warriors in the service of King David, are identified as "Ithrites" (2 Samuel 23:38 and 1 Chronicles 11:40, which gives the same list). Once the word designates the clan itself: in 1 Chronicles 2:53, the "Ithrites" are listed as one of the families settled in Kiriath-jearim, a town in the territory of Judah. This usage shows that the term served to identify a person's genealogical origin or to name a family group settled in a region.
